CrowdStrike’s Zscaler deal is a $44B vote for platformization and a long-term threat to Palo Alto Networks

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, the security industry has told buyers to choose best-of-breed security products, leaving practitioners to stitch them together.
  • This has been perpetuated by the major analyst firms, which have a Wave for this product and a Magic Quadrant for that product.
  • Recent findings suggest that palo Alto Networks Inc.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:11 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

For decades, the security industry has told buyers to choose best-of-breed security products, leaving practitioners to stitch them together.

This has been perpetuated by the major analyst firms, which have a Wave for this product and a Magic Quadrant for that product. The reality is that choosing best-of-breed everywhere has never led to best-in-class threat protection.

Recent findings suggest that palo Alto Networks Inc. has long articulated the value of security platformization. To be precise, Fortinet Inc. was the first vendor to advance the concept of a security platform, but no security provider has pushed the industry as hard as Palo Alto. Chief Executice Nikesh Arora has been vocal about platforms as the only way to truly protect the entire attack surface.

In a recent development, crowdStrike Holdings Inc.’s agreement to acquire Zscaler Inc. for $43.9 billion strongly supports the thesis. SiliconANGLE has been covering the deal, so I won’t rehash the details. In short, the leader in endpoint security is buying the leader in cloud-delivered zero-trust access. The combined company is expected to start with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue, and the deal is expected to close between August 2027 and January 2028.

Over the long term, the combination poses a real threat to Palo Alto. In the short term, it is a strong co-sell opportunity for CrowdStrike and Zscaler, with significant integration work between the two.

Arora has long argued that customers want fewer vendors and integrated platforms. Getting there can be challenging, as security teams often operate with an “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” mentality. The mere thought of replacing a working product is enough to keep even the most seasoned security pros up at night. In February 2024, when he cut guidance to fund the platform push, Palo Alto’s stock fell 28% in a day. Since then, the stock has recovered nicely, validating his strategy, and its rival has now raised $44 billion to head down its own platform journey.

Recent findings suggest that in some ways, CrowdStrike and Zscaler were the strongest argument against platformization, though one could argue that each was its own smaller “platform,” depending on how you define it. Each led its category, and the two were close partners, with more than 2,000 shared customers and 16 product integrations. If best-of-breed products, tied together by integrations, could work anywhere, it was here. The two companies are now taking it a step further. “When you integrate as partners, there’s only so much you can do,” Zscaler founder and CEO Jay Chaudhry remarked on the analyst call.

Recent findings suggest that the “why now?” question is worth asking, as the coming together of these two companies has been rumored for some time. The answer is that agentic AI creates fresh challenges and risks that are difficult to address through a partnership. An AI agent runs on a device and then crosses the network to access models, tools, and data, operating at machine speed around the clock. A vendor that sees only the device or only the network sees only half of what the agent does. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said adversaries are “exploiting the seams and the gaps between companies’ integrations.”.

I agree. Every seam between products is a place for an attacker to hide, and AI-driven attacks exploit those seams faster than security teams can close them. But a platform is more than one vendor and one contract. It means one dataset, one agent, and one policy engine, so a detection on a laptop triggers enforcement across the network without a person in the middle. If that’s the standard, CrowdStrike, while it currently describes itself as a platform, is not today.

With Zscaler, CrowdStrike is more than just a product to fill a gap. Zscaler is a best-in-class Secure Access Service Edge stack that protects half of the Fortune 500 and runs what it calls the world’s largest inline security cloud.

Sources indicate that it is also built for resilience, which matters more than ever. Last week, I wrote about six major outages over six days at organizations ranging from Microsoft to the Federal Aviation Administration. Zscaler sits between every user and every application, so if it fails, the business stops. That has forced the organization to engineer for failure.

Its Business Continuity Cloud provides each customer with a dedicated backup environment in third-party data centers, on separate networks and DNS, with software updates deliberately staggered so a bad release can’t affect both simultaneously. “No linkage — no network, no shared routers, no switches, no shared network operations,” Chaudhry told me in a previous conversation.

Industry observers note that of all companies, CrowdStrike should value that. In July 2024, a faulty Falcon update affected an estimated 8.5 million Windows devices. The standard objection to platformization is concentration risk, and it intensifies when a single vendor controls both the endpoint agent and the path to every application. Zscaler’s continuity design is the best answer to that objection I’ve seen, and CrowdStrike should extend it across Falcon.

The near-term value is commercial. CrowdStrike notes about 8,000 Zscaler customers don’t yet buy from it. Channel partners already sell both companies, and the two sales teams already work deals together.

After the close, Zscaler will transition to Falcon Flex, CrowdStrike’s licensing model. “A Zscaler customer can add Falcon. A Falcon customer can add Zscaler. One contract, one platform,” Kurtz remarked. CrowdStrike expects about $1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing.

This target seems bullish but achievable, as it requires no code integration — only sales execution, which both companies are good at.

In a recent development, today, the Falcon sensor and Zscaler’s client run as separate agents on separate clouds with different release schedules. Kurtz promised that it will collapse into one. “The brand promise, single agent, that’s not going to change,” he said. CrowdStrike’s next-generation sensor can already inspect and proxy network traffic, he added, which should make the job easier.

Industry observers note that kurtz was also candid about the effort: “Yes, there’s hard work to be done. There always is in an acquisition.” CrowdStrike gave no timeline. The engineering teams can’t combine until the deal closes, which is at least eight months away. CrowdStrike’s largest prior acquisition cost less than $1 billion. Folding Zscaler’s global security cloud into Falcon is far harder than anything it has attempted. Until that work is done, the platform exists on slides.

That gap gives Palo Alto time to further its own platform. It closed its CyberArk acquisition in February, renamed the business Idira, and is already cross-selling it to its existing customers.

In a recent development, the long term looks different. If CrowdStrike delivers a single agent and a single dataset, Palo Alto will face something it hasn’t had: a rival of similar scale with the leading endpoint product and the leading zero-trust cloud on one platform. Palo Alto is most exposed in SASE, where its Prisma SASE business has been chasing Zscaler.

CrowdStrike plus Zscaler make a formidable platform, but it still lacks a firewall. Zscaler is a cloud proxy, and many enterprises that use it still run firewalls in their data centers, campuses, and clouds. That is Palo Alto’s core area of strength.

It has been revealed that looking ahead, that should open the door to another acquisition. Check Point is the obvious choice, as it will struggle over the long term as a firewall pure-play in a market shifting to platforms, and it would give CrowdStrike a large installed base. If CrowdStrike wants a broader networking portfolio, Fortinet is the bigger swing, with switching, wireless and software-defined wide-area network alongside its firewalls. The two already partner on endpoint and firewall protection.

Recent findings suggest that either deal would add more integration work to Zscaler, so I wouldn’t expect either to happen soon. But a organization that wants to displace Palo Alto can’t leave the firewall to someone else forever. I understand zero trust can replace a number of firewalls, particularly in branch offices, but firewalls are here to stay for the foreseeable future.

The deal also puts smaller security vendors in play. Netskope and Cato Networks are both independent SASE vendors competing against a bundle, and Oppenheimer has already named Netskope an attractive target.

Fortinet is an obvious acquirer, but the buyer pool extends beyond security companies. Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., following its acquisition of Juniper Networks Inc., is embedding security across its network and may seek to bolster that portfolio. Dell Technologies Inc. lags in security, with a portfolio centered on data protection and resilience, and could benefit from an acquisition to close the gap.

Sources indicate that nothing changes today, and customers shouldn’t pause their projects. I’d use the waiting period to prepare in advance.

Buy what is integrated. Ask for the integration roadmap with dates for the single agent, the shared data set and unified policy. Until those ship, evaluate CrowdStrike and Zscaler as two products.

Use leverage. Palo Alto is trying to pry Zscaler accounts loose, and CrowdStrike and Zscaler want commitments before the close. As Sanchit Vir Gogia of Greyhound Research told CSO, “Consolidation is sold at the first signature and priced at the second.” Negotiate price caps for renewals now.

Get interoperability in writing. When asked about lock-in, Kurtz noted, “We have and will continue to work well with all of the other technologies and ecosystem.” If you run Zscaler with another endpoint product or Falcon with another access provider, include that promise in your contract.

Make resilience a requirement. Ask CrowdStrike to commit to maintaining Zscaler’s Business Continuity Cloud and its staggered updates, and to apply the same discipline to a combined agent.

This deal settles the argument over platformization. Who wins is still unclear. CrowdStrike has to do the integration work, and Palo Alto has the better part of a year to persuade customers not to wait. The great news for customers is that big moves like this create a wave of innovation. AI is changing security faster than ever before, and a CrowdStrike-vs.-Palo Alto battle is good for everyone.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#111475. Breaking: Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms

Breaking: Stanford scientists discover hidden brain signals that predict Alzheimer’s years before symptoms

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Subtle patterns of brain activity may reveal the risk of Alzheimer's disease years before memory problems develop or harmful proteins begin accumulating in the brain, according to new research led by Stanford Medicine.
  • In a recent development, the study, published November 4 in Science Advances, points to a potentially powerful newly introduced way to detect early warning signs of cognitive decline.
  • Industry observers note that to investigate, the research team examined brain activity in adults aged 75 and older who represented opposite ends of the cognitive aging spectrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Subtle patterns of brain activity may reveal the risk of Alzheimer's disease years before memory problems develop or harmful proteins begin accumulating in the brain, according to new research led by Stanford Medicine. The same approach can also identify people whose brains show exceptional resistance to cognitive decline, suggesting they may eventually become "super agers.".

In a recent development, the study, published November 4 in Science Advances, points to a potentially powerful newly introduced way to detect early warning signs of cognitive decline. Unlike conventional biomarkers, these patterns of brain activity might eventually be possible to change through targeted interventions.

Industry observers note that to investigate, the research team examined brain activity in adults aged 75 and older who represented opposite ends of the cognitive aging spectrum. One group had Alzheimer's disease, while the other consisted of super agers, older individuals whose memories remained comparable to those of people decades younger. Using the differences between these groups, the scientists created a scoring system to evaluate brain activity in cognitively healthy adults between 55 and 70.

Sources indicate that the results revealed a striking connection between brain activity and future cognitive health. People whose brain patterns more closely resembled those of Alzheimer's patients were more likely to experience cognitive decline, accumulate amyloid-beta plaques, and receive an Alzheimer's diagnosis during follow-up periods extending up to 12 years. Those with activity patterns resembling super agers were more likely to maintain their cognitive abilities and avoid these outcomes.

A Newly introduced Way to Detect Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss.

The latest scoring system predicted future cognitive decline more effectively than several established indicators, including demographic characteristics, genetic risk factors, and amyloid-beta and tau biomarkers. This suggests that examining how different regions of the brain communicate could reveal Alzheimer's risk earlier than existing approaches.

Sources indicate that "We want to address a major challenge in the Alzheimer's field nowadays -- most studies are looking at well-known Alzheimer's disease biomarkers, such as amyloid-beta or tau. But those are observable at relatively late stages of the disease," said Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences and senior author of the study. "What we really care about is defining early markers that can detect earlier signs of cognitive decline and potentially help us deliver timely interventions to people.".

Sources indicate that zhang envisions a future in which treatments could potentially move someone's brain activity toward the patterns associated with greater cognitive resilience. Possible approaches include cognitive training and transcranial magnetic stimulation, which uses magnetic pulses to influence brain activity.

Transcranial magnetic stimulation has already demonstrated potential for changing brain activity in people being treated for depression. However, neither of these proposed approaches has been tested in this context for preventing cognitive decline, and researchers do not yet know whether changing brain activity would alter the course of Alzheimer's disease. The upcoming findings provide a starting point for identifying which brain regions might be useful treatment targets.

"There are two main components: One is to know which part of the brain to target, the other is how we should change it," Zhang said. "That's why identifying the super-ager brain resilience pattern is a critical component -- so we know what a good pattern should be.".

What Makes Super Agers' Brains Different?

Depending on how they are defined, approximately 10% of older adults may qualify as super agers. For this research, the term referred to people at least 75 years old who performed on memory tests at a level typical of a 45-year-old while maintaining normal executive function for their age.

In a recent development, scientists have become increasingly interested in these unusually resilient individuals. Most earlier studies, however, compared super-agers with other older adults who performed normally on cognitive assessments.

It has been revealed that zhang recognized that this approach could overlook notable biological differences. Two people might receive similar scores on memory tests despite having very different underlying brain health. One might already be developing amyloid-beta plaques or showing other biological changes associated with aging, while the other might not.

"Normal, cognitively unimpaired individuals are pretty heterogeneous in terms of their biological abnormalities," he remarked. "Simply comparing super agers with such a heterogeneous population makes it challenging to define what is critical in terms of resilient or vulnerable brain patterns.".

In other words, comparing super agers with a broad mixture of seemingly healthy older adults makes it difficult to determine which brain characteristics actually protect against decline.

Industry observers note that the Stanford team took a different approach. Rather than using typical older adults as the comparison group, they examined people with Alzheimer's disease who were approximately the same age as the super agers. This created two more clearly defined groups at opposite ends of the cognitive spectrum.

Brain Scans Reveal a Hidden Pattern.

The researchers drew on imaging information collected through several major research initiatives, including the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies, the Harvard Aging Brain Study, and the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.

According to recent reports, they examined resting-state functional MRI scans from 180 super agers and 110 people diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. This imaging technique records patterns of brain activity while a person lies quietly inside a scanner.

Sources indicate that the comparison uncovered distinctive differences in activity across multiple brain regions. Some areas showed greater activity while others showed reduced activity, producing recognizable patterns that distinguished the two groups. Scientists refer to the relationships among these regions as functional connectivity, or the functional connectome.

Sources indicate that using these patterns, the team developed a measurement called the Alzheimer's resilience-vulnerability connectome, or ARC score. This scoring method distinguished super agers from Alzheimer's patients with approximately 85% accuracy.

The researchers then investigated whether the same brain signature could help predict what would happen to people who had not yet developed any noticeable cognitive problems.

Predicting Alzheimer's Risk Years in Advance.

In a recent development, the team applied the ARC scoring system to more than 1,300 cognitively healthy adults between the ages of 55 and 70. Their scores fell across a broad range, with lower values reflecting brain activity more similar to super agers and higher values indicating patterns closer to those observed in Alzheimer's patients.

According to recent reports, at the beginning of the study, people with high and low ARC scores highlighted no obvious differences in cognitive performance. As researchers examined follow-up data collected over subsequent years, however, crucial differences became apparent.

"We used the ARC score to make a prediction of how likely this patient will convert into mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease," said Kanhao (Alex) Zhao, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar in psychiatry and lead author of the study.

Recent findings suggest that the available follow-up periods differed across the datasets. Some participants had records extending as long as 12 years, although most were tracked for approximately five to six years. Even within these shorter periods, the initial ARC scores helped predict subsequent changes in cognitive abilities.

Sources indicate that people whose scores indicated more Alzheimer's-like brain activity experienced more rapid declines on standard tests of memory, attention, and executive function. In contrast, those with patterns most similar to super agers generally experienced the slowest cognitive decline.

"We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer's disease," Zhao noted. "Our model reveals comparable or better prediction ability, and it can do so at an earlier time point. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves.".

A More Precise Measure of Brain Aging.

Industry observers note that the team also investigated how ARC scores related to another measure of neurological health called brain age. This measure estimates brain aging using functional MRI information collected from healthy individuals.

Although the two measurements demonstrated some correlation, Zhang emphasized that ARC provides more targeted information about a person's vulnerability or resistance to cognitive decline during aging.

"I'm excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline," he said.

The findings suggest that patterns of communication between brain regions may offer valuable information about future cognitive health that cannot be captured through standard memory testing alone.

They also raise the possibility that combining brain activity measurements with established Alzheimer's biomarkers could improve the identification of people who would benefit most from earlier monitoring or future preventive treatments.

Could Brain Training Help Prevent Alzheimer's?

Despite the encouraging results, researchers caution that ARC scores are not intended to diagnose Alzheimer's disease. For now, the system should be viewed as a potential tool for tracking cognitive health and estimating future risk.

Zhang also stresses that a person's score is not a permanent prediction of their future. Brain activity can change over time, and an individual who initially indicates a resilient pattern may not maintain it indefinitely.

Industry observers note that for example, the proportion of people with super-ager-like ARC scores generally declines with advancing age. Brain injuries and neuropsychiatric conditions can also influence the patterns associated with cognitive resilience.

It has been revealed that importantly, this potential for change may work in both directions. If brain activity can shift toward patterns associated with vulnerability, Zhang hopes future treatments might also encourage it to move toward greater resilience.

His research team is preparing a trial that will measure ARC scores before and after cognitive training. The goal is to explore whether targeted training can influence the brain activity patterns associated with healthier cognitive aging.

It has been revealed that "But the critical part is that we have to intervene at an early stage," he remarked. "That's why we focus on the cognitively unimpaired population to identify super-ager-like versus Alzheimer's-like individuals. If we can precisely identify such as early indicator, I'm optimistic that we can reverse or prevent this process through advanced intervention technologies.".

Industry observers note that although it remains unknown whether modifying these brain patterns can prevent or delay Alzheimer's, the discovery offers a potentially important latest direction for research. By identifying differences in brain activity before symptoms emerge, scientists may eventually gain a valuable opportunity to intervene while cognitive function is still intact.

Researchers from Children's National Hospital; the University of Texas at Austin; Lehigh University; Penn State College of Medicine; Latest York University Grossman School of Medicine; and the University of California, Los Angeles also participated in the research.

Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health (grants R21AG080425, R01MH129694 and R01AG081768), a joint Rosenkranz Foundation-Knight Initiative program, an Alzheimer's Association grant, and a Lehigh University CORE grant.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jennifer Garner is getting a head start on Christmas at her Los Angeles home, where thousands of lights are already twinkling and monogrammed stockings hang above the fireplace.
  • The 54-year-old actress shared a look at her holiday decorations on Instagram, revealing that even her greenhouse got a festive touch with a wreath of its own.
  • Industry observers note that thanksgiving preparations were underway in the kitchen, where Garner gave the turkey a trial run ahead of the big day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jennifer Garner is getting a head start on Christmas at her Los Angeles home, where thousands of lights are already twinkling and monogrammed stockings hang above the fireplace.

The 54-year-old actress shared a look at her holiday decorations on Instagram, revealing that even her greenhouse got a festive touch with a wreath of its own.

Industry observers note that thanksgiving preparations were underway in the kitchen, where Garner gave the turkey a trial run ahead of the big day. Her dogs and cat were dressed for the occasion, too, in turkey costumes.

“We’re ready over here,” Garner wrote in the caption.

Garner has been known to love the holiday season, having previously opened up about her favorite memories during a Nov. 4 episode of the "Happy Hour With Ina Garten" podcast.

“My favorite Thanksgivings were when my kids were really little, I think it was right at the end of 'Alias,' and it was at a big house,” remarked Garner, who shares Violet, 20, Seraphina, 17, and Samuel, 14, with her ex-husband Ben Affleck.

“My kids were little, and Ben and I were there, and we all cooked. Bradley made the stuffing and Victor made ... I think Victor’s sister came. It was just our little 'Alias' family cooking together. It was so special," she added, referring to her co-stars Victor Garber, Ron Rifkin, and Bradley Cooper.

Despite separating in 2015 and divorcing in 2018, Garner and Affleck have continued to celebrate the holidays together.

Last year, a source told People that the couple spent the holidays together in Los Angeles.

“Jen makes it very special. She’s such a great chef. She loves having her whole family together, too. Ben’s always welcome at her house,” the source told the outlet.

Garner is known for showing off touching memories at her dwelling.

Last year, Garner and her mom were brought to tears when they were surprised with a near-perfect re-creation of the kitchen that sat inside the actress' childhood home in West Virginia.

Garner and her mom, Patricia Ann, couldn't help but get emotional when they were brought to the space, which had been designed by appliance tech giant KitchenAid to perfectly mirror the kitchen of their Charleston, WV, home.

The mother-daughter duo initially thought they were being brought in to take part in a holiday photo shoot, but after stepping inside the kitchen set, which looked identical to the one in their Greystone Place abode, they were left gobsmacked.

Both Garner and her mom began welling up at seeing their vintage wooden table and green refrigerator, with both women promptly recalling the happy memories they had made in the original space.

“This is where we would hang out, all our crafts happened right here with somebody looking through from that side," Garner said, while looking through the cupboards. "This is the cabinet where you hid the chocolate chips.".

The kitchen boasted a large wooden table, matching wooden cabinets, yellow oven, granite countertops, drawings, and a yellow KitchenAid mixer.

Industry observers note that the "13 Going on 30" star then pointed at a nostalgic photo of her mom that was placed on the counter. It reminded her of the days that Patricia would get her perm done while "sitting at the table.".

“It’s a privilege to get to see where we used to be. I want that to be the den, and then I want to hear dad come home from work. That’s what I feel," Patricia noted.

The 87-year-old noted that the patterned wallpaper in the replica kitchen first caught her eye.

Garner noted that the experience gave her a "really deep feeling of homesickness and gratitude.".

Patricia previously joined her daughter on Garner's latest installment of her "Pretend Cooking Show.".

  • The offering, called Aetna For You and Baby, will be available to all expectant mothers enrolled in an Aetna plan.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Aetna unveils new program aimed at offering end-to-end support for moms and babies" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Aetna is rolling out a upcoming program that aims to provide key end-to-end care for pregnant women, new mothers and infants.

The offering, called Aetna For You and Baby, will be available to all expectant mothers enrolled in an Aetna plan. Through the program, moms will be connected to a prenatal visit in their first trimester and a postpartum visit within 12 weeks of the baby's birth.

Women in the program will also be screened for depression both during and after pregnancy to identify any risks.

In addition to supporting the mother both during pregnancy and postpartum, the program aims to give babies a healthy start by providing at least six well visits through their first 15 months, which offer critical tests and screenings, checkups and vaccinations.

The news of the launch was provided first to Fierce Healthcare.

Katerina Guerraz, Aetna's chief operating officer, told Fierce that maternal care often focuses mostly, if not completely, on labor and delivery, though prenatal and postpartum visits play a critical role in driving positive health outcomes.

In its announcement, Aetna notes that data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show that about 90% of pregnancy-related deaths could have been prevented, with a lack of access to prenatal care and more complete support making for a key barrier.

"This is a national access issue, a quality issue, and it's an affordability problem," she said.

In addition, it's not uncommon for programs that aim to drive better maternal outcomes to lack services for the babies, who in the first year of life undergo a wide array of critical developmental milestones, Guerraz said.

Aetna, as the third-largest insurer in the U.S., sees about 200,000 deliveries a year among its members. That means the success of this program could have a significant impact in a short amount of time, supporting at least 1 million babies over the next five years, she remarked.

Aetna for You and Baby also builds on a broader push within the company to build a more personalized and simple experience for members. For instance, the company established a program that embeds Aetna nurses in the hospital to support discharge planning and transitions for members, and Guerraz said that holds potential in the maternal care space.

For example, if a baby needs to stay in the neonatal intensive care unit after birth, having an Aetna nurse in the NICU providing additional support to the clinical team and the member would pay dividends, she said.

Aetna is also plugged into Health 100, a sister subsidiary of its parent company, CVS Health, that offers an AI-powered tool to help patients identify healthcare costs and navigate their benefits, even if they're not members of Aetna or Caremark or CVS Pharmacy customers.

Guerraz noted the program is designed to offer something that patients can carry with them if their coverage changes.

She added that the team intends to continue iterating on the program and identifying other barriers to care for moms and their babies.

"This is something that we know is going to have a massive impact," she noted.

Latest Update: A new fiber supplement could help millions suffering from irritable bowel syndrome

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A specially designed fiber supplement may offer a promising fresh way to improve gut health for millions of people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
  • The research team at ECU's Nutrition and Health Innovation Research Institute (NHIRI) found that the supplement, called ur gut®, improved gut health in people with IBS without increasing abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation.
  • Industry observers note that IBS affects people around the world, including nearly 11 percent of Australians.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A specially designed fiber supplement may offer a promising fresh way to improve gut health for millions of people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Researchers at Edith Cowan University (ECU) have developed and tested a fiber combination that supports beneficial gut bacteria without making common digestive symptoms worse.

The research team at ECU's Nutrition and Health Innovation Research Institute (NHIRI) found that the supplement, called ur gut®, improved gut health in people with IBS without increasing abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, or constipation.

Industry observers note that IBS affects people around the world, including nearly 11 percent of Australians. Although its exact cause remains unclear, stress, infections, and certain medications may contribute to the condition. Symptoms can also become worse because of particular foods, inadequate sleep, psychological stress, hormonal changes, and lifestyle factors.

Why Common IBS Diets Can Affect Gut Health.

Recent findings suggest that people with IBS are frequently advised to follow a low-FODMAP diet, which limits certain carbohydrates that are easily fermented by gut bacteria. Although this approach can help control uncomfortable symptoms, restricting these foods may also have unintended consequences for the gut microbiome.

Industry observers note that "For years we've known that a diet low in Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monesaccharides and Polyols (FODMAPs) can relieve symptoms, but they can also reduce beneficial gut bacteria and negatively impact fiber intake over time," lead author Dr. Tina Yan said.

"We wanted to find a way to build better gut health while following a low-FODMAP diet.".

The new findings suggest that a carefully formulated fiber supplement could help address this problem, allowing people with IBS to support a healthier gut microbiome while continuing to manage their symptoms through dietary changes.

The researchers attribute the supplement's promising effects to its combination of two ingredients: resistant starch and psyllium husk.

Psyllium appears to slow the breakdown of resistant starch by gut bacteria, allowing more of it to reach deeper sections of the colon before fermentation occurs. This process may increase the production of beneficial compounds that support intestinal health.

Ordinarily, fermentable fiber can be challenging for people with IBS because bacterial fermentation can produce excess gas and increase digestive discomfort. The new formulation appears to offer a way to obtain the benefits of fermentation without aggravating these symptoms.

Sources indicate that "Traditionally, fermentable fibers can be difficult for people with IBS because they can increase gas production and discomfort," Dr. Yan remarked.

"What's exciting about this study is that participants maintained stable symptoms while showing meaningful improvements in their gut microbiota as well as in their gut-related anxiety.".

Significant Changes in Gut Bacteria and Anxiety.

The researchers observed substantial shifts in the composition of participants' gut bacteria during the intervention. These changes were particularly notable because they occurred over a relatively short period.

"Changes of this magnitude are rarely seen with such a short intervention," ur gut® co-creator Professor Amanda Devine remarked.

"The study demonstrated that our targeted dietary fiber blend positively reshaped the gut microbiome in people with IBS following a low-FODMAP diet, supporting beneficial bacteria linked to gut and mental health. This was great to see.".

Industry observers note that alongside improvements in gut bacteria, participants also experienced reductions in gut-related anxiety. These findings suggest that the supplement's potential benefits may extend beyond changes in the digestive system, although further research will be needed to establish its broader effects.

A Newly introduced Approach to Managing Irritable Bowel Syndrome.

The researchers believe their findings could help shift IBS care toward improving the underlying health of the gut rather than focusing exclusively on avoiding foods that cause discomfort.

"For many people with IBS, success has traditionally meant simply avoiding certain foods," ur gut® co-creator Associate Professor Claus Christophersen said.

"Our findings suggest we may also be able to actively rebuild gut health and the microbiome while not making IBS symptoms worse. That's an crucial step forward.".

By demonstrating that beneficial gut bacteria can be supported without increasing IBS symptoms, the study points toward new dietary strategies that could complement existing treatments.

The ur gut® supplement is already available for purchase. The research team has also created a cookbook featuring recipes designed to help people incorporate the supplement into a healthy diet.

The study, "Dietary fibre blend improves gut health in patients with irritable bowel syndrome following a low FODMAP diet: a randomised, double-blind control trial," was published online in the European Journal of Nutrition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Healthcare purchasers must weigh hospital quality alongside their prices, Leapfrog says" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Patient safety watchdog The Leapfrog Group released its latest collection of hospital safety grades hand-in-hand with calls for policymakers and stakeholders to consider, or directly tie patient safety reporting to price transparency.

Sources indicate that the twice-yearly release brought top marks for 900 out of a total 2,366 graded hospitals, and the lowest “F” score for just three. There were 774 hospitals that earned a “B” grade, 655 a “C” grade, and 35 a “D” grade.

No grades were assigned to another 447 hospitals, a decision the group made after a judge’s ruling in a lawsuit involving the scores it would assign to facilities that did not voluntarily submit their quality data to Leapfrog’s survey (Leapfrog appealed that decision in September). Leapfrog’s decision not to score these has generally shifted its letter grade distribution upward, and the organization has stated it is reviewing a potential methodology change for upcoming gradings to incorporate non-submitting hospitals.

Still, “a record number of hospitals are choosing to publicly report their safety and quality performance, and we applaud them for holding themselves accountable to their patients,” Leapfrog President and CEO Leah Binder remarked in a statement.

Industry observers note that at the state level, Connecticut maintained its claim on the largest portion of hospitals earning an “A” grade (64.3% of its total), followed by Utah, New Jersey and South Carolina. Leapfrog also called out Rhode Island and Maine for jumping up the rankings—from eighteenth to seventh for the former, and from seventeenth to eighth for the latter. No hospitals were given an “A” grade in five states: Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming.

A hospital’s assigned grade is calculated by reviewing recent data on up to 22 patient safety measures, including a 10-part Medicare composite of reported patient safety and adverse events. Safety scores for specific hospitals can be searched on the group’s website.

Leapfrog and Binder, in a news release outlining its latest scores, made the case that its grades and similar independent measures warrant a seat at the table in a transparency conversation primarily focused on hospital costs.

“Progress on price transparency is vital, but there’s no good price for bad care,” Binder remarked. “We are calling on the Trump Administration and Congress to ensure price transparency is integrated with patient safety and quality transparency.”.

The group backed its calls by pointing to a recent analysis (PDF) conducted by the Purchaser Business Group on Health (PBGH) that reviewed employer claims, federal price transparency data, and quality and safety measures including Leapfrog’s. It “found little to no correlation between negotiated prices and standardized quality measures,” as hospitals that received high safety grades often charged cheaper prices than those in the same market with lower grades.

Leapfrog and Elizabeth Mitchell, president and CEO of PBGH, mentioned the analysis—currently being expanded for practical usage by healthcare purchasers—is an example of how a more wholistic view of prices and care delivery should be considered when weighing a hospital.

“Employers have an appropriate duty to pay a fair price for high-quality care, and they can’t meet it by looking at price alone,” Mitchell remarked in the release from Leapfrog. “When we put the data together, some of the most expensive hospitals were not the safest. Our members want to buy high-quality, safe care that is fairly priced. That shouldn’t be too much to ask.”.

#111467. Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't

Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1420 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A growing body of research suggests that aging may be more flexible than once believed.
  • Their findings suggest that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests.
  • The findings, published in Nature Medicine, could help scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments more effectively, although researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean people will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A growing body of research suggests that aging may be more flexible than once believed. Now, scientists at Yale have taken an important step toward identifying which treatments can actually influence biological aging and which ones show little measurable benefit.

Their findings suggest that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests. Popular over-the-counter supplements examined in the research, however, indicated little evidence of producing the same effects.

The findings, published in Nature Medicine, could help scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments more effectively, although researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean people will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.

From Fighting Cancer to Understanding Aging.

In a recent development, when Raghav Sehgal began graduate school at Yale several years ago, he planned to use advanced computer science techniques to investigate cancer. His background in engineering and experience launching a computational biology startup had given him a strong foundation for that work.

Recent findings suggest that however, a question from his Ph.D. adviser at the Yale School of Medicine changed his research direction. Rather than focusing on individual diseases such as cancer or cardiovascular disease, why not investigate the aging process that contributes to their development?

In a recent development, "That put me on a different path," mentioned Sehgal, now an associate research scientist in psychiatry who specializes in computational biology and bioinformatics. "As researchers, we have a long way to go in understanding the aging process and whether the steps we take to manage it really work.".

Sources indicate that sehgal now studies the biological mechanisms behind human aging, how scientists can measure those changes, and why getting older increases the likelihood of conditions such as cancer, diabetes, and dementia. His work also explores whether interventions might reverse certain aspects of biological aging, even if eliminating aging itself remains beyond reach.

Fresh DNA Tests Reveal Which Anti-Aging Treatments Work.

Industry observers note that sehgal is the lead author of the newly introduced study, which was conducted in the laboratory of Albert Higgins-Chen, an assistant professor of psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine. The research team set out to determine which existing approaches to slowing aging produce changes that can be reliably measured.

Their analysis found encouraging results for certain medications and lifestyle interventions. In contrast, the over-the-counter supplements included in the study generally failed to produce meaningful reductions in biological age.

The project involved the entire Higgins-Chen laboratory, including Daniel Borrus, Jenel F. Armstrong, John Gonzalez, Jessica Kasamoto, and Yaroslav Markov.

Industry observers note that "For the first time we've shown that certain therapies have measurable impacts," said Sehgal. "This wasn't previously possible, because we didn't have enough data to say these biomarkers are consistently responsive to these interventions.".

It has been revealed that biomarkers provide measurable information about what is happening inside the body. In aging research, they can help estimate a person's biological or functional age, which may differ from their chronological age.

How Scientists Measure Biological Age.

To investigate whether treatments could influence aging, the Yale team relied primarily on blood-based measurements called epigenetic clocks.

These tools analyze chemical patterns attached to DNA, particularly methyl groups (basic chemical structures that act like tags). Previous research has shown that these chemical markers change as people grow older. Some interventions may reverse certain age-associated patterns, and computer algorithms use those changes to estimate a person's biological age.

In a recent development, the researchers brought together findings from 51 clinical studies investigating different anti-aging strategies. These ranged from dietary supplements and medications to lifestyle changes and medical procedures.

Across those studies, the team examined more than 110 DNA methylation biomarkers (including 16 major epigenetic clocks). By comparing measurements taken before and after interventions, they could evaluate which approaches were associated with reductions in biological age.

In a recent development, "What we did was pretty unique," Sehgal said. "We already know that certain things might prolong health span and lifespan. There is data from retrospective analysis as well as from animal models. We took all that knowledge along with the real-world clinical studies to identify which interventions in humans were slowing down aging across the board in these known biomarkers.".

Which Anti-Aging Treatments Indicated the Best Results?

The researchers divided the interventions into four main groups: prescription drugs, lifestyle modifications, over-the-counter supplements, and medical procedures.

It has been revealed that one of the clearest findings involved diet and exercise. Combining regular physical activity with a healthy eating blueprint consistently reduced epigenetic age. The dietary approaches examined included Mediterranean, low-fat, and low-carb diets.

The strongest reductions in biological age markers were associated with certain pharmaceutical treatments. These included metformin and semaglutide, prescription medications used to manage metabolic conditions and body weight, as well as anti-TNF therapies that target a protein involved in the body's inflammatory response.

(TNF, or tumor necrosis factor, is an immune-system protein that helps fight inflammation-related injury.).

The findings were less encouraging for over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures. In the studies examined, these approaches did not produce measurable reductions in epigenetic age.

The researchers also discovered that newer biological age clocks performed better than older versions. Another crucial finding was that people living with diseases generally experienced larger changes in their aging biomarkers than healthy participants.

Could DNA Blood Tests Transform Anti-Aging Research?

According to Sehgal, the next priority is to test these findings in larger, more diverse populations. This would help researchers determine how consistently different treatments influence biological aging across people with different health conditions and backgrounds.

The improved blood tests could also dramatically shorten the time needed to evaluate potential anti-aging therapies.

"If these new biomarkers are eventually validated to predict long-term health, scientists will be able to evaluate anti-aging therapies much faster," he added. "Instead of waiting decades for evidence from clinical trials, we'll be able to see which interventions are effective and in which people in a few years or even months.".

That possibility could represent a major advance for aging research. Instead of relying entirely on clinical studies that follow participants for decades, scientists might eventually use validated biological age measurements to identify promising treatments much earlier.

However, senior author Higgins-Chen stressed that scientists must be careful about interpreting what changes in aging biomarkers actually mean.

In a recent development, "We have developed a rigorous, systematic approach to evaluating and comparing how biomarkers change across a wide variety of interventions, and that is a critical step in the right direction," he noted. "However, the true meaning of that change must be fully understood.".

Important Questions About Slowing Aging Remain.

Although the results are promising, several major questions remain unanswered.

For example, researchers still need to establish whether changes in biological age are directly caused by a treatment or influenced by other factors that were not accounted for. They also need to understand how swiftly those changes occur, whether they persist after treatment ends, and which biological processes produce them.

Most importantly, scientists have not yet established whether lowering epigenetic age leads to meaningful improvements in long-term health.

"And most importantly - what does the change mean for our long-term risk of age-related disease and functional decline?" Higgins-Chen stated.

Further investigations into these questions are underway, with additional studies led by Borrus, Armstrong, and Grace Zou.

The Higgins-Chen laboratory is also affiliated with Yale's Department of Pathology, the Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Program, and the Y-Age Yale Center for Research on Aging.

What Appears to Work Against Biological Aging?

Based on the improved DNA-based blood tests, the Yale researchers identified two particularly promising approaches for reducing biological age markers:.

The analysis also identified benefits from certain anti-TNF medications, while the tested over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures showed little measurable effect.

Recent findings suggest that these results provide a clearer picture of which interventions may influence biological aging. However, more research is needed to confirm the findings and determine whether reductions in biological age markers ultimately translate into fewer age-related diseases, better health, or longer lives.

Latest Update: Cisco and OpenAI launch Shirudo open-source infrastructure shield to prevent AI-driven cyberattacks

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1196 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that cybercriminals have gained the ability to discover vulnerabilities in software and take advantage of them in seconds, and it’s all thanks to artificial intelligence.
  • According to recent reports, they’ve just unveiled a latest, open-source and extremely ambitious initiative called the Secure Infrastructure Project, which aims to ensure that all AI computing infrastructure is secure by design and capable of defending against lightning-fast AI-driven attacks.
  • In a blog post, Cisco Security Chief Technology Officer and Vice President of Engineering Thomas Graf explained that the industry has always treated security as an afterthought, essentially something that’s bolted onto systems after the fact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:20 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Industry observers note that cybercriminals have gained the ability to discover vulnerabilities in software and take advantage of them in seconds, and it’s all thanks to artificial intelligence. Enterprises need a better way to defend themselves, so it’s fitting that one of the world’s top AI companies, OpenAI Group PBC, together with Cisco Systems Inc., is stepping up with a solution.

According to recent reports, they’ve just unveiled a latest, open-source and extremely ambitious initiative called the Secure Infrastructure Project, which aims to ensure that all AI computing infrastructure is secure by design and capable of defending against lightning-fast AI-driven attacks. The first project within that initiative is Shirudo, which is designed to protect infrastructure systems automatically from critical exploits before they can be patched.

In a blog post, Cisco Security Chief Technology Officer and Vice President of Engineering Thomas Graf explained that the industry has always treated security as an afterthought, essentially something that’s bolted onto systems after the fact. It has gotten away with this because much of the world’s computing infrastructure was built for workflows that proceed at human speeds. But with the emergence of AI models that can discover and work out how to exploit vulnerabilities in a matter of seconds, this kind of reactive security is no longer enough.

According to Graf, even now, when a major vulnerability is discovered in widely used software, it can take weeks or even months to come up with a fix and ensure that every major system is patched against it. “That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative, meaning that a growing number of vulnerabilities are now being exploited before they are publicly disclosed,” he said. “This will only accelerate with the further evolution of AI models and cybersecurity capabilities, becoming the norm in open-weight models.”.

It has been revealed that to counter these kinds of automated attacks, Cisco and OpenAI believe that infrastructure has to be rebuilt from scratch with security in mind. They argue that it’s time to abandon static defenses and embrace systems that are hardened by default, immutable and rebuildable from a previous “good” state, so people can swiftly revert back in the event of an attack. To do this, infrastructure systems must be based on Trusted Platform Modules and utilize reinforcement learning techniques to safely test their own defenses so they can adapt when faced with novel cyberattacks from previously unknown vectors.

Graf remarked the key to doing this is to secure workloads at runtime, which is why the initial focus of Cisco’s and OpenAI’s initiative is Shirudo, an evolution of the open-source Tetragon runtime security project that aims to provide autonomous defense for AI agents.

Shirudo, named after the Japanese word for “shield,” is based on extended Berkeley Packet Filter or eBPF, which is a Linux kernel technology that acts like a kind of sandbox within the operating system. Similar to how JavaScript makes web browsers programmable without a restart, eBPF enables small, verified programs to run inside the Linux kernel to observe an application’s activity and modify its behavior without altering its source code or rebooting it.

Industry observers note that graf explained that Cisco and OpenAI chose to use eBPF because there are no other real alternatives. Human-focused security consoles and policy languages are simply too slow for AI agents, and will limit their productivity.

By exposing programmable kernel interfaces, eBPF enables AI agents to capture granular telemetry, evaluate mitigations in monitoring mode and deploy cryptographically-signed shields in milliseconds. So cyberattacks that exploit unknown vulnerabilities can be blocked in real time without causing disruption to their live workloads.

In a recent development, “There is nothing more important than giving security teams the tools they need to match the speed of the AI-driven threats they are facing,” mentioned Cisco President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel. “We need self-defending infrastructure that acts at the speed of code, learns in real time and shields itself until patches are safely rolled out.”.

According to recent reports, openAI’s role in this is to prove that eBPF is up to the job, and it has already deployed Shirudo as part of an agentic control plane that’s powered by its Codex coding agent. When given details of a newly introduced vulnerability, Codex can use Shirudo to autonomously build an exploit reproducer and then design a mitigation strategy. It then validates the mitigation code and deploys the cryptographically-signed shields across all affected nodes.

The two partners recently tested Shirudo against a critical latest vulnerability in OpenJDK called Java4Shell, and it was able to rapidly generate Java bytecode that it injected directly into a running Elasticsearch agent to block malicious Base64 overwrites that would have compromised the system.

OpenAI co-founder and President Greg Brockman mentioned the goal of Shirudo is to help companies protect their systems from newly introduced threats until they can build and deploy a more durable patch. “When one team finds a better way to protect a system, others shouldn’t have to start from scratch,” he explained.

To that end, Cisco and OpenAI say they’re welcoming developers, kernel engineers, platform builders and security experts to collaborate on Shirudo and other initiatives within their broader Secure Infrastructure Project.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Florida court tosses Tampa General Hospital's suit against Eli Lilly over 340B discounts" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A Florida federal court has tossed Tampa General Hospital's lawsuit against Eli Lilly over the 340B drug discount program.

Florida's Middle District court dismissed the case on a motion from the drugmaker on Wednesday. If Tampa General Hospital wants to file an amended complaint, it must do so within 30 days.

The hospital initially sued the pharmaceutical firm over a policy it implemented that requires providers to submit claims-level data on pharmacy and medical dispensing if they participate in 340B. Lilly said it would pull back discounts for providers that did not comply with the requirement and has done so for several organizations, drawing ire from the industry.

Tampa General stated the decision is "unconscionable and immoral" in the initial complaint, filed in July.

It has been revealed that however, the district court argued that Supreme Court precedent holds that organizations like hospitals do not have the private right to sue if they have been charged beyond the threshold, based on a 2011 decision. SCOTUS stated that the right to sue was not outlined by Congress, so it is not an avenue available to these organizations.

"The Court made clear that there is simply no private remedy to superintend the pricing and provision of these discounted drugs," per the order.

"To permit this suit would be to encourage piecemeal litigation and defeat the [Supreme] Court’s insistence on maintaining the Congressional strategy 'harmoniously and on a uniform, nationwide basis,'" according to the document.

Eli Lilly cheered the decision in a statement.

Sources indicate that "Today’s decision is an important step toward a more transparent 340B program," a Lilly spokesperson noted. "Lilly’s claims data requirement asks hospitals for basic information—information they already give insurers every day—to prevent unlawful duplicate discounts.".

Industry observers note that "Decades of HRSA guidance and two federal appeals courts confirm that Lilly can lawfully require this information," the drugmaker remarked. "More than 3,200 hospitals and clinics already share it with Lilly, and we hope Tampa General Hospital will join them.".

Tampa General Hospital has sued Eli Lilly and Tech giant over the drugmaker’s “unconscionable and immoral” rescindment of discounted pricing under the 340B program.

Recent findings suggest that the complaint, filed last week for the U.S. District Court in the Middle District of Florida, is early legal fallout from a policy Lilly implemented earlier this year that requires providers participating in the federal subsidy program to submit claims-level data for all pharmacy and medical dispensations. The company threatened to pull the discounts for those that didn’t comply and made good on its threat for a subset of hospitals last month, sparking outrage among provider groups.

Tampa General, a nearly 1,000-bed disproportionate share hospital, confirmed in the legal complaint that it was among those cut off. It is now spending 25% to 50% more on average for Lilly products, “many of which it must purchase because of Lilly’s status as the market’s only supplier of a given drug product.”.

Sources indicate that tampa General’s lawsuit frequently describes Lilly in such terms, framing the drugmaker as holding significant monopoly power and wielding it in violation of the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. It also often draws contrast to the 340B program’s intent to support the margins of safety-net hospitals providing care to vulnerable patients, against Lilly’s current status as the largest pharmaceutical tech giant in the world by market cap.

A spokesperson for Lilly, in a statement given to Fierce Healthcare, described the lawsuit as “just another part of the broader hospital campaign to fight transparency and hide the fraud, waste and abuse that plague the 340B program.”.

According to recent reports, tampa General asked the court to order an immediate end to Lilly’s policy and to award damages for the higher prices to which the hospital was subjected. It contends Lilly’s alleged failure to comply with 340B pricing requirements and decision to continue marketing its products as 340B-discounted are unfair trade practices under the Florida statute.

“The most valuable pharmaceutical manufacturer in the world is engaged in a campaign to transfer dollars earmarked for charitable purposes into its own pocket,” the complaint reads. “The direct and inevitable result of Lilly’s actions is reduced healthcare for poor people. Its actions shock the conscience and are self-evidently unconscionable.”.

Tampa General, similar to the hospital associations that have protested Lilly’s policy, contends that the claims data it requires imposes substantial administrative burden on 340B providers. Even “hospitals who have caved to Lilly’s newly introduced demands” have effectively had the prices for their covered outpatient drugs increased due to those administrative costs, it wrote in the complaint.

Lilly and other drugmakers who have signaled similar prepares have mentioned they need claims data to spot instances in which a drug purchase is improperly granted multiple discounts under overlapping programs. The organization has also disputed that the burden of its policy is as substantial as hospitals say.

Sources indicate that “The claims data Lilly requires hospitals to share is information they already collect and send to insurers regularly,” the Lilly spokesperson said of the lawsuit’s claims. “Refusing to share that same data with Lilly indicates that hospitals are more concerned with hiding rampant abuse in the program than improving its integrity. Lilly will keep working to ensure this program serves vulnerable patients instead of hospitals and their for-profit partners.”.

The 340B program has proven to be a magnet for industry and policy conflict, particularly in recent years as its scale has ballooned. The divide is most evident in the ongoing clash over a pilot rebate program that the Trump administration attempted to launch at the top of the year but was forced to restart after the hospital industry’s legal pushback.

340B providers also received a shock this past week when the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services floated a significant reduction in its 340B reimbursement to 33.4% below average sales price in its annual proposed rule on hospital outpatient payments.

AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1700 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, more than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year.
  • Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.
  • According to recent reports, the discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, more than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

According to recent reports, the discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss.

The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

According to recent reports, another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely latest type of medical test.

The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

Sources indicate that "Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops.".

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict.

Recent findings suggest that sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

Industry observers note that immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

According to recent reports, because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late.".

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening.

It has been revealed that doctors presently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things.".

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns.

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

In a recent development, "Good AI starts with good data," remarked Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a substantial part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today.".

Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

Industry observers note that "It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer stated. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a significant return when they get over the finish line.".

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments.

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Industry observers note that obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal Fresh Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer noted, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening.".
