Engel & Völkers declared an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

It has been revealed that brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into latest markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it looks to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Recent findings suggest that engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, mentioned in a statement.

It has been revealed that realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the firm. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa noted in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Sources indicate that jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Sources indicate that baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Industry observers note that dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs remarked in a statement.

Industry observers note that IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the manufacturer.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter remarked in a statement.

#111351. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1343 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Redfin ↗ Open Full Page

Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Redfin

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that just three of the 50 most populous U.S.
  • It has been revealed that nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers.
  • According to recent reports, all three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

It has been revealed that nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

According to recent reports, all three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

According to recent reports, the seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

It has been revealed that “Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” stated Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially key to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”.

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

Sources indicate that when sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

According to recent reports, we estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

Industry observers note that it’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

According to recent reports, “A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan noted. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate. With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”.

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more newly introduced listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

In a recent development, some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

According to recent reports, the Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add upcoming homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

In a recent development, demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

According to recent reports, the surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jessica Alba’s divorce from Cash Warren is back in the headlines after a latest court order awarded Warren $577,481 from Alba’s retirement benefits.

The ruling comes after the former couple sold their longtime Beverly Hills–area home and Alba later purchased another property in the area.

The retirement award comes from Alba’s account in the HonorBar Inc. Profit Sharing Plan, according to court documents reported by TMZ.

In a recent development, any money left in the account after Warren receives his share is to go to Alba. The documents also allow Warren to take the award as a lump sum or move it into an individual retirement account or another retirement blueprint.

The court order also addresses account records: If Warren requests statements in writing within the next year, Alba must provide them within 10 days.

According to the outlet, transferring the money into a retirement account could avoid a 20% tax withholding.

The ruling is the latest financial development following the couple’s divorce, which was finalized in February 2026.

It was previously reported that Alba was ordered to pay Warren $3 million to balance the division of their assets.

Their settlement also divided interests in several companies, shares in The Honest Company, and residuals from projects made during their marriage.

Meanwhile, Alba and Warren have already put their real estate ties behind them.

Their former Beverly Hills–area home was sold in 2025. Alba and Warren purchased the seven-bedroom estate for $9.9 million in 2017, then put it on the market in April 2025 for $18.99 million. It was sold for $18.2 million, with the closing recorded on June 27, 2025.

The property sat on about 1.86 acres and included 8.5 bathrooms, a guesthouse, a home theater, and extensive grounds.

Alba and Warren undertook an 18-month renovation after buying it, with Alba involved in decisions about the home’s design.

The estate had been a family residence for years, and Alba spoke about the family’s intends for the house during a 2019 Architectural Digest tour.

After the sale, Alba picked up a splashy Beverly Hills estate in September 2025 for $4.75 million.

The roughly 5,000-square-foot property boasts four bedrooms, five bathrooms, tiled roofing, and modern amenities.

The two transactions mark a change in Alba’s recent housing history: the end of her and Warren’s ownership of a sprawling family estate, followed by her purchase of another Beverly Hills property.

Alba and Warren announced their separation in December 2024 after 16 years of marriage.

Alba filed for divorce citing irreconcilable differences, and the sale of their longtime home followed the announcement.

The latest retirement-benefit order concerns a separate part of their financial settlement, while the Beverly Hills transactions provide a look at the real estate changes that accompanied their split.

UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Exposure management tech giant Astelia Inc. today confirmed the launch of autonomous network mitigation, a upcoming capability that allows organizations to block artificial intelligence-driven exploits at the network level, even when a patch isn’t available or can’t be applied.

In a recent development, the latest capability has been designed to address what Astelia claims is the problem of frontier AI models cutting the time to exploit to almost zero, leaving manual triage and remediation unable to keep up. Astelia argues that autonomous remediation isn’t a viable option for large enterprises, where every patch requires a change window so it doesn’t break crucial business processes. In many cases, there is also no patch to apply because the vendor hasn’t released a fix yet or, for older and end-of-life systems, never will.

“For years, security teams have been told to patch faster,” remarked co-founder and Chief Executive Alon Noy, adding that the advice “stops working when the exploit arrives before the change window does.”.

Autonomous network mitigation is designed to block the path an attacker would use to reach a vulnerable system instead of changing the system itself. Mitigations are applied automatically within policies the organization sets. Nothing on the asset is changed, allowing business-critical systems, including operational technology, to stay online.

In a recent development, underpinning the service is Astelia’s reachability analysis, which maps an organization’s real network topology and applies agentic AI to analyze the requirements of each exploit. By correlating exploit conditions with network topology, the platform identifies which vulnerabilities are reachable by attackers and through which paths. In one enterprise deployment, approximately 40 million vulnerabilities were reduced to fewer than 2,000 that were reachable, according to the organization.

Sources indicate that key features of autonomous network mitigation include the ability to identify the most effective choke point on an attack path and drive the mitigation through an organization’s web application firewall or intrusion prevention and detection system. A single rule at a choke point is said to protect every vulnerable server behind it, compared with one change per server when patching. Because mitigations are only applied to paths that have been proven reachable, the service doesn’t add rules for exposure that doesn’t exist.

Every mitigation applied by Astelia can also be rolled back, something that isn’t always possible with a patch. That is noted to allow teams to act quickly without putting business operations at risk.

Recent findings suggest that autonomous network mitigation can be deployed through Astelia Agents, the company’s suite of AI agents, as a dedicated agent that applies mitigations on its own. The agent can also be connected with other agents to respond to urgent threats such as zero-day vulnerabilities and critical disclosures. Astelia gave the example of the PHP2Shell remote code execution flaws disclosed in October, which left end-of-life PHP servers with no official fix.

Each organization sets its own guardrails on how mitigations are applied. Customers can require human approval for specific environments or actions, according to the organization. Every action is logged and can be audited. Analysis on the Astelia platform continues to run on read-only integrations, with mitigation actions using scoped permissions that each organization enables and controls.

Autonomous network mitigation initially supports web application firewall and intrusion prevention and detection rules, with support for firewall rules planned in the future.

Founded in 2024 by former leaders of the Israeli National Red Team, Astelia is a venture capital-backed company that raised $35 million in combined seed and Series A funding in February. Investors in the company include Index Ventures, Team8 and Holly Ventures.

Jumping out of a helicopter into water below, rappelling down a 22-story building, enduring chemical warfare gas exposure — if you’ve never seen Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test, these are just a few of the tasks that must be completed.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a reality TV show in which celebrities do physical challenges from the actual Special Forces selection process playbook. It’s like a competition show, but there are no eliminations, and no one gets voted off.

To leave, participants must voluntarily withdraw, be medically withdrawn by a DS (directing staff) due to injury or be dismissed for refusing a direct order. During the final test, the DS ejects those who fail the interrogation or selection test.

Season 5 is set in the Malaysian jungle. It features Candace Cameron Bure, Brandi Glanville, Oliver Hudson, Ruby Rose, George Santos, Bre Tiesi, Matt Barnes, and Mauricio and Alexia Umansky, among others.

Recent findings suggest that at the time that this article was published, Alexia was still in the competition. Alexia agreed with the decision, saying the gas was the “most painful thing” she’d ever experienced in her life.

Inman spoke to Mauricio and Alexia midway through the season about the experience, the latest industry news and what’s next for The Agency.

In a recent development, I believe sellers should have choice, but I believe that we should be sharing those private listings amongst everybody — every agent, every brokerage firm, not just keeping it for themselves. I feel like there’s a lot happening right now in the industry where everybody’s really looking out for themselves: the MLSs, NAR, Compass.

Actually, Compass, I think, wants to collaborate, wants to share, but they’re in a big, big fight. But in the meantime, this Clear Cooperation Policy is what is allowing them to keep all the listings to themselves and not share them … The PLS is exactly what that was, and I still think that if Clear Cooperation Policy didn’t pass, it would have been an amazing business to have right now.

Mauricio: We are really positioned as the premier luxury brokerage firm outside of Compass right now. They’ve got Sotheby’s, they’ve got Christie’s, they’ve got all of those different brands, and we’re the only independent luxury brokerage firm out there right now.

So I’m excited to be in that position. Competitors make you better every single day … I’m excited in terms of where we sit, where we stand in a very difficult time; I’m not excited about the market. We really need to do some things to improve it. We’ve had three years of very, very difficult conditions, and it’s going to be very difficult for people to survive. And those that do survive will come out better.

It has been revealed that I think we’re in a good position to survive, but we’ve got our work cut out for us over the next year, year and a half. But we’ll continue to grow. We’ll continue to expand, and I’m excited to just be a part of this industry. But man, it’s hard out there right now.

#111344. Tech Report: We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (966 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople.
  • I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since.
  • According to recent reports, you didn’t fail the program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

According to recent reports, you didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

The reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

According to recent reports, nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

Industry observers note that that is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

This isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

According to recent reports, we all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

In a recent development, now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

Industry observers note that the veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Industry observers note that somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

We do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

Industry observers note that what would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

That work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

According to recent reports, we haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

In a recent development, we’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

You aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

According to recent reports, lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” takes place in the Theranos founder’s former Del Mar, CA, rental—and the property’s location in an exclusive, gated community could be just part of the reason the film’s unexpected release was such a smash.

The project—which is now available to stream on demand and was directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim—was kept secret for the four years it was in production, leaving viewers in awe after the documentary’s surprise Sept. 6 premiere at Telluride Film Festival.

Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, invited the film crew—which Oppenheim told Variety was intentionally kept intimate to keep the project a secret—to reside in the guesthouse of the home for the 34 days before she reported to Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, TX, on May 30, 2023.

“Keeping it under wraps was very important because we never wanted to get in front of what we were capturing,” the director shared.

The crew would typically shoot for 16-hour days, with Fielder telling Variety that cameras were strategically positioned to “cover the whole house” so nothing would be missed.

The four-bedroom, four-bathroom beachfront property is located in an ultraprivate community less than a half-hour from San Diego. Called Sandy Lane, it features just about a dozen residences.

“This is basically a hidden community. It’s a guard-gated community, which is so rare on a beach, which is why you have a lot of high-profile individuals up and down this strip,” celebrity real estate agent Josh Altman explained in a home tour of another property on the community’s sole street.

Given the home's private location—and considering California’s anti-paparazzi legislation protecting private property from capture—it’s plain to see why Holmes and Evans opted to rent the 2,200-square-foot dwelling in the time leading up to her imprisonment.

According to recent reports, the Upcoming York Times also previously reported that the couple and their two children moved to the area to be nearer to Evans’ family. His parents, William L. Evans and Susan Evans, are the hotel magnates behind Evans Hotels, a San Diego–based hospitality company.

Although the property is presently off-market, a previous listing indicates the single-story home was built in 1948 and includes direct access to the private beach.

As seen in the film, the abode features tall ceilings with exposed-beams and sizable windows connecting the home to the serene surrounding landscape. Midcentury modern design is present throughout the home, which is paneled in honey-hued wood.

While Realtor.com® estimates the property’s current market value to be about $5.8 million, it’s unclear just how much Holmes and Evans shelled out to reside there temporarily. The most recent publicly listed rent was $5,650 a month in 2015, which is a decrease from the $5,950 rent it was listed for in 2012.

In a recent development, the Sandy Lane spot is not the only prominent rental property Holmes has retreated to since her legal troubles began. During her trial from Aug. 31, 2021, to Jan. 3, 2022, she resided in one of the seven homes of San Francisco’s notable Green Gables.

The sprawling 74-acre property was owned by the Fleishhacker family for over a century before it was sold for a record-breaking $85 million in 2025.

Before Theranos came crumbling down, Holmes and her former business and romantic partner, Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, purchased a $9 million French provincial manor in Atherton, a wealthy enclave of Silicon Valley.

Privacy was likely a factor in that decision, as well, as the five-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom mansion was set behind a gated entrance and tall trees.

The home was considerably more lavish than the beach bungalow that serves as the backdrop for “You Can See Everything,” with a 6,800-square-foot main home accompanied by gardens, a pool, and a pavilion on a 1.16-acre lot.

Along with the couple’s young children, Evans has since relocated from California to Texas, so the family can visit Holmes in prison, where she is serving an 11-year sentence for three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

The sentence was reduced to nine years for good behavior, and Holmes has since been approved for placement in a community correction center, ABC News reported, citing an enhancement from the Department of Justice's Victim Notification System.

Holmes is scheduled to be placed in the Austin Transitional Center in De Valle, TX, in August 2027.

Tech Roundup: Zillow Preview listings go live in RealScout

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1136 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.
  • This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s new monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.
  • It has been revealed that lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s new monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

It has been revealed that lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

It has been revealed that “Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

The time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

For real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

Sources indicate that the money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

Debt was a big part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and stated the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on new real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and new ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb plans to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the company stated in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

Industry observers note that instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment concerns, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

“Travel is aspirational,” Chesky said. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”.

The announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the firm’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first announced in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

Preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

Sources indicate that “Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner said in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”.

Sources indicate that for agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:23 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Intelligent data infrastructure is becoming a priority as enterprises move artificial intelligence beyond isolated pilots and into production environments.

The shift places fresh demands on storage systems built to support traditional applications, especially as organizations introduce AI workloads across hybrid and multicloud environments. NetApp Inc. is responding with a strategy that emphasizes infrastructure modernization without requiring enterprises to abandon existing investments, according to George Kurian (pictured), chief executive officer of NetApp.

Sources indicate that “I think that the AI era requires organizations to be really good stewards of their data, because data is the foundation for knowledge and knowledge is the intellectual property,” he told theCUBE. “To have knowledge, you need really good intelligent data infrastructure that not only allows you to extract memory and context from your data, but also to keep it secure, well governed and a resource that you can trust.”.

Recent findings suggest that kurian spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand and co-host Rebecca Knight during NetApp INSIGHT, in an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The event’s coverage featured NetApp executives and technology partners discussing the evolving demands on enterprise data infrastructure and the challenges of bringing AI into production. (Disclosure below.).

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with George Kurian:.

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT:.

According to recent reports, enterprise AI workloads are exposing limitations in storage architectures designed for more predictable application demands. NetApp’s Novus architecture separates data and metadata management so each can scale independently. The manufacturer’s AI Data Engine is designed to discover, classify and prepare enterprise data for AI applications, according to Syam Nair, chief product officer of NetApp.

“Performance and throughput of accessing the data, that’s a necessity for AI, but that won’t be sufficient for agents to actually act on the data,” he remarked during the event. “If the data is not ready and it’s not protected, you get fast results. You get compromised results, but they may not be the ones you want.”.

In a recent development, the demands of AI factories are also changing how storage resources must be managed. NetApp’s approach aims to support high-throughput AI pipelines without sacrificing the responsiveness other applications require, according to Arindam Banerjee, chief platform and technology officer of NetApp, who spoke alongside Jason Hardy, vice president of storage technology at Nvidia Corp.

Sources indicate that “What happens is [that] different types of workloads like transactional workloads for metadata and heavy sequential workloads for, say, checkpoints, happen at the same time,” Banerjee told theCUBE. “Previous architectures did one or the other very well. They never were able to combine it and do both at the same time.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jason Hardy and Arindam Banerjee:.

Modernizing enterprise infrastructure often requires organizations to accommodate existing applications while introducing newly introduced AI capabilities. NetApp and Oracle Corp. are addressing that challenge through a co-engineered, fully managed storage service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

Sources indicate that “When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most key thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”.

In a recent development, netApp and Oracle Corp. are extending enterprise storage capabilities into the public cloud through a co-engineered, fully managed service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

Sources indicate that “When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most vital thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”.

Sources indicate that the integration challenge extends beyond cloud storage to the networking and compute resources that support AI workloads. NetApp and Cisco Systems Inc. are expanding their FlexPod infrastructure with validated designs intended to reduce deployment complexity. The partnership has served 10,000 customers over 16 years, according to James Cole, vice president of data center networking, business development, partnerships and go-to-market at Cisco, and Alvaro Celis, chief partner and ecosystem officer at NetApp.

“Twenty years ago, 10 years ago, you would’ve been designing your data structures and your applications around the infrastructure. Now we’ve turned that on its head,” Cole stated during the event. “You’re really designing the infrastructure around the movement of data. Who better to do that together than the person you trust with your data and the person you trust with your network?”.

According to recent reports, another partnership focuses on private AI deployment and measurable business outcomes. The NetApp AIPod Mini combines NetApp infrastructure with the Generate platform from Iterate Studio Inc., doing business as Iterate.ai, according to Brian Sathianathan, co-founder and chief technology officer of Iterate.ai. In one insurance deployment cited during the discussion, an agent reduced accident-report analysis from approximately eight hours to eight minutes.

According to recent reports, “AIPod Mini has attached connections to the NetApp storage, and it talks to NetApp using the ONTAP protocol that’s time-tested,” he noted during the event. “Then, on top of the AIPod Mini, we are running our Generate software. That software has a [large language model] embedded in it, so you can run all your AI queries locally and fully privately within your four walls.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Alvaro Celis and James Cole:.

As enterprises introduce autonomous agents into infrastructure management, intelligent data infrastructure must accommodate increasingly complex operational demands. NetApp’s unified control plane, delivered through NetApp Console, is designed to reduce routine administrative work through policy-driven automation. In one keynote demonstration, agents responded to a nighttime performance anomaly, according to Sandeep Singh, senior vice president and general manager of enterprise storage at NetApp.

“Agents can, in real time, implement the necessary quality of service rules to ensure there’s compliance to the boundary conditions there,” he told theCUBE. “And that way, no human is woken up. The right outcome is achieved, and there’s no noisy neighbor effect. And there’s an audit trail presented to the humans for going and following up.”.

Automation, however, can’t resolve organizational questions about data ownership and responsibility. As enterprises extend intelligent data infrastructure across applications and environments, leadership must establish accountability for the information those systems rely on, according to Helen Yu, founder and chief executive officer of Tigon Advisory Corp., who appeared alongside Singh.

“It’s not a storage problem. It’s a leadership and accountability issue,” she said during the event. “When teams don’t have access to … trusted data consistently, they actually stop making decisions. They start making workarounds.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Helen Yu and Sandeep Singh:.

#111340. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2160 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Redfin ↗ Open Full Page

The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Redfin

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right?
  • The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing.
  • In a recent development, boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

In a recent development, boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Sources indicate that key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In a recent development, in their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

According to recent reports, two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

It has been revealed that “For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s key to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”.

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another substantial expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Sources indicate that baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao remarked. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”.

Industry observers note that that dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze demonstrates up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Generations are defined by birth year:.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:.

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Sources indicate that share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

Industry observers note that how to read the results by age. Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. Existing-home sales sink to a 16-year low as mortgage rates bite

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.
  • Existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million).
  • Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

Existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun remarked mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Industry observers note that fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

“Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun remarked in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”.

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

It has been revealed that “There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant mentioned in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”.

Yun and Sturtevant mentioned mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

Recent findings suggest that “So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant mentioned. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”.

Added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”.

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

Industry observers note that as a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun said, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

Sources indicate that “Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he said. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”.

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

“If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun said in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”.

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale stated existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

“Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she noted. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”.

Hale mentioned jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

“[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she stated. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”.

Yun said rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

In a recent development, “One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he remarked. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the major change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”.

However, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she remarked. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on fresh pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that what do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

Industry observers note that on this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

He explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel notable.

They also get into handling rejection, taking big risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

Shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy indicates many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

For agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

His advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:19 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Cloudera Inc. today announced a digital sovereignty package that it said enables organizations to maintain control over their data, artificial intelligence models and computing infrastructure regardless of where workloads run.

Cloudera for Digital Sovereignty combines the company’s Anywhere Cloud, Open Data Lakehouse and Unified Data Fabric technologies with open-weight AI models and model customization tools from Mistral AI SAS, with whom Cloudera recently partnered. The integrated offering supports deployment across sovereign clouds, private data centers and fully air-gapped environments that have no connection to external networks.

Digital sovereignty is becoming a more pressing issue as enterprises move beyond managing data residency to ensuring that the AI models and infrastructure they depend upon remain under their control. McKinsey & Co. reported last year that 71% of the executives it surveyed called sovereign AI an “existential concern” or “strategic imperative.” Cloudera stated its own research found that regulation, privacy and data sovereignty requirements rank among the top three barriers to scaling AI.

“As AI becomes more autonomous and embedded in critical operations, enterprises need to know that their data, models, and infrastructure can remain under their control even as technology and regulatory requirements change,” Cloudera Chief Technology Officer Sergio Gago said in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that the offering provides consistent zero-trust access controls, data lineage tracking and governance policies across deployment environments. Those capabilities are intended to help organizations address requirements imposed by the European Union’s AI Act, Digital Operational Resilience Act and Network and Information Security Directive, among other regulations.

Sources indicate that governance policies also extend to the enterprise data that AI agents retrieve and use in performing tasks. Mistral’s open-weight models can run alongside governed data, enabling organizations to customize models locally and execute agentic workflows without exposing sensitive information.

It has been revealed that cloudera’s modular hybrid cloud architecture enables people to shift computing workloads between infrastructure providers and private data centers without rewriting applications or migrating or duplicating underlying data. Organizations can also selectively apply sovereignty controls to sensitive workloads without imposing the same restrictions across their entire computing estate.

Industry observers note that moor Insights & Strategy Inc. Chief Analyst Patrick Moorhead noted AI has raised the bar on data protection. “A company can meet every line of its sovereignty policy and still not control who accesses its data or who can turn off the models it depends on,” he said in a statement.

Industry observers note that cloudera noted it will supplement its Mistral partnership with an ecosystem of sovereign cloud providers and implementation partners. The company is initially targeting Europe but plans to expand the partner network into other regions and regulatory jurisdictions.

  • The Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027.
  • Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of big news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

The Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

Recent findings suggest that investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are New York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.
