Industry News: Iowa Residents Told To Evacuate or Shelter in Place as U.S. Army Prepares To Detonate Nearly 10,000 Pounds of a Lead Explosive

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Army intends to detonate 9,700 pounds of a lead-based explosive in Southeast Iowa on Wednesday, despite concerns from environmental groups.
  • The detonation is scheduled to go ahead at 10 a.m.
  • Two rapid, controlled detonations were initially scheduled to take place last Friday, but the plans were pushed to Wednesday due to a combination of public concern and weather optimization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Army intends to detonate 9,700 pounds of a lead-based explosive in Southeast Iowa on Wednesday, despite concerns from environmental groups.

The detonation is scheduled to go ahead at 10 a.m. on Wednesday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, IA. This comes after a lawsuit was filed by the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter asking the federal appeals court to halt the plan.

Two rapid, controlled detonations were initially scheduled to take place last Friday, but the plans were pushed to Wednesday due to a combination of public concern and weather optimization.

Set to be detonated are 68 drums of degraded lead azide, adding up to roughly 9,700 pounds, which have become sensitive and unstable. It is the primary explosive used to initiate munitions.

A controlled detonation is now the only viable option, according to the Army’s Q&A page about the event.

As lead azide degrades, it crystalizes and becomes sensitive to temperature changes, shock, and friction, making it unsafe to move. There are chemical neutralization procedures, but the drums are too unstable for the physical manipulation this option requires, according to the Army.

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Region 7 Director Jim Macy wrote a letter to Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, ensuring her that the EPA was working alongside the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the Department of Defense to ensure the controlled detonation was “conducted in the safest manner possible.”.

“All agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” Macy wrote in the letter, according to the Iowa Capital Dispatch.

In a recent development, an updated public safety advisory shared by the Army on Tuesday shared the agency’s plans to make the detonation as safe as possible. The lead azide will be detonated in earth-covered magazines, which are built for the purposes of holding ammunition and explosives, and are reinforced.

Additional physical barriers made of sand, a “water wall,” gel blocks, and aqueous foam barriers will be in place to contain particle dispersion, absorb thermal energy, and reduce airborne particulate dispersal. These measures, as well as drone surveillance of lead levels, are in place to track and minimize deposition outside the plant.

The Army has acknowledged that lead particles will impact communities outside the plant. It has defined an evacuation zone as a "5-mile cone extending southwest of IAAAP.".

Those in the evacuation zone will be provided short-term hotel lodging, food, water, and transportation as needed.

It has also laid out recommendations for those outside the evacuation zone, such as sheltering in place, closing all windows and doors, and setting heating to recirculate and avoid pulling in air from outside.

Still, environmental groups are concerned about the lead plume, which they say could spread 100 miles, depending on weather conditions.

"The EPA itself admits that there is no safe level of lead exposure for humans," said Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, in a press release shared with Realtor.com®.

"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal.".

The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, Iowa Chapter, were only made aware of the unprecedented detonation plan early last week, initially scheduled for Friday. In response, the groups filed a lawsuit on Thursday challenging the permit that the EPA issued the Army.

“Based on the information that was made public at the time, which was very little information, there were serious concerns about the effectiveness of the public notification and the information being put out to protect the public,” Thien Chau, a senior attorney at Earth Justice, tells Realtor.com.

“There were serious concerns about the mitigations measures in place to reduce the impact as well as to properly do remediation and cleanup and address any harm that people may face from the impact of the detonation.”.

Many local lawmakers were not made aware of the controlled detonation either, and were only informed about the looks and risk once the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra club told them, despite the widespread impact on surrounding communities, according to Chau.

“That’s why we filed the lawsuit: to make sure that all the information and resources and capabilities that could be provided were provided to the people potentially impacted by this,” states Chau.

In a recent development, “Since that filing, a lot of things have happened. The government has put out a lot more information, and while we expect a detonation to take place this Wednesday, we are glad to see that because there was additional time, there are now additional mitigation measures and resources have been provided for potentially impacted people.”.

According to recent reports, the Department of Justice responded in opposition to the lawsuit. Both the DOJ and Army maintain that a controlled detonation is the safest option and further delay, especially with cold weather approaching, could lead to a natural, uncontrolled detonation, which would be more difficult to mitigate.

“The Army has delayed detonation by three days now,” the DOJ’s brief remarked. “But every day of delay increases the risk of an uncontrolled explosion that will cause far greater public health and environmental harm than the planned, controlled detonation initiated under the protective terms of the Permit.”.

#111332. The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (760 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (760 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients.
  • Sources indicate that ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place.
  • Wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients. Here’s how the multi-market real estate agent combines local expertise with a connected brokerage network.

Sources indicate that ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place. A primary home in Los Angeles, a ski house in Aspen, a pied-à-terre in New York, a winter retreat in Miami or the Caribbean.

Wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it. The agents who serve these clients best are evolving alongside them, building expertise across markets and cultivating relationships that extend well beyond their own backyards.

Sources indicate that that shift is changing what it means to be a local expert. For brokerage leaders, it also raises an important question: Are we building networks that reflect how our clients actually live?

Remote work, flexible schedules and a generation of buyers who think of themselves as global citizens have loosened the link between where someone earns, where they live and where they invest.

Today’s luxury buyers are driven by lifestyle, whether that means access to mountains, water, a particular school system or a city’s cultural calendar, and they are comfortable buying in places where they spend only part of the year. What has not changed is their expectation of personalized service.

For these clients, a traditional handoff creates friction. Each time they are passed from one agent to another, they repeat their goals, rebuild trust and wonder whether anyone sees the full picture. A client’s real estate portfolio is one story. Their advisor should be able to tell it across markets.

Going global does not mean going generic. A Manhattan co-op board, a Florida insurance requirement, a Colorado water right and a California disclosure obligation each carry real consequences, and clients need professionals who understand the market in which they are buying or selling.

Industry observers note that the mistake is confusing geographic reach with geographic expertise. The strongest multi-market agents know where their knowledge is deepest and where collaboration adds value. The future of the multi-market real estate agent isn’t about being an expert everywhere. It’s about knowing where your expertise ends, who to bring into the conversation and how to make that collaboration seamless for the client.

When a client has a positive experience with an agent in one city, that relationship shouldn’t end at the city limits. But there is a meaningful difference between providing a referral and extending a trusted relationship. If an agent simply passes along a name, the client starts over. If that introduction comes with shared context and a clear understanding of the client’s priorities, the experience feels seamless.

Trust is portable, but only when it is supported by consistent service and relationships built before a client needs them.

A global footprint alone does not create a global client experience. Offices in multiple markets mean little if they operate independently. Brokerages need to provide the infrastructure that makes cross-market relationships work, including introductions between offices, shared market intelligence, consistent training and clear expectations around communication and referrals.

It has been revealed that at The Agency, we encourage agents to bring colleagues from other offices into client relationships early, so clients experience a connected team rather than a series of separate introductions. Technology helps agents share insights, access inventory and present properties remotely, but the real advantage comes from the relationships behind it.

Recent findings suggest that start by looking at the markets that consistently appear in your referral activity and client conversations. Those patterns show where to build stronger partnerships between offices.

Invest in cross-market education so agents recognize regional nuances and regulatory considerations and know when to bring in specialized expertise. Set clear collaboration standards for how clients are introduced, who takes the lead and how agents stay involved. Then measure success beyond the transaction: Did the client feel supported, and was communication consistent?

As brokerage leaders, we should be asking whether our networks are simply growing in size or becoming more connected. Those are very different measures of success.

In a recent development, local expertise has never been more valuable. What is changing is its reach. The brokerages that treat their agents’ knowledge as a connected network, rather than a set of separate territories, will be better positioned to serve today’s clients and the next generation of buyers who increasingly see the world, not one city, as their real estate market.

#111331. If the AI Bubble Pops, Here’s What It Means for Your Home’s Value

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1652 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Realtor ↗ Open Full Page

If the AI Bubble Pops, Here’s What It Means for Your Home’s Value

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When artificial intelligence giant Anthropic went public last week, its $1.494 trillion valuation exceeded the combined value of every owner-occupied home in the San Francisco metropolitan area, according to research from Realtor.com®.
  • Less than a week later, the organization's shares fell below their IPO price, as a renewed sell-off in tech stocks stoked fears that the AI bubble may already be bursting.
  • “This is how the exuberance ends—not with a whimper but with a bang,” Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman wrote on Monday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When artificial intelligence giant Anthropic went public last week, its $1.494 trillion valuation exceeded the combined value of every owner-occupied home in the San Francisco metropolitan area, according to research from Realtor.com®.

Less than a week later, the organization's shares fell below their IPO price, as a renewed sell-off in tech stocks stoked fears that the AI bubble may already be bursting.

“This is how the exuberance ends—not with a whimper but with a bang,” Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman wrote on Monday.

Krugman, who warned of America's housing bubble as early as 2005, acknowledges he's less certain about AI valuations than he was about home prices two decades ago. But earlier this month, he warned that an AI bust would almost certainly trigger a recession, potentially more painful than the one that followed the dot-com crash.

Others on Wall Street aren't so sure. Many investors remain confident in the industry's fundamentals and see the sell-off as a necessary correction rather than the end of the boom.

But after years of a bull market powered by a handful of AI darlings, newly introduced research from Realtor.com finds evidence that the resulting fortunes have helped shape some of America’s most expensive housing markets.

Now, a reversal of those gains could threaten a source of wealth far more central to the financial lives of middle-class Americans: their homes.

Anthropic's IPO alone was expected to mint around 2,800 millionaires among its current and former employees, according to estimates from private-market research firm Sacra reported by Reuters.

But Americans needn't work in AI or invest in individual tech stocks to have shared in the windfall. Between the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022 and Nov. 3 of this year, the S&P 500 gained nearly $32 trillion in market value—more than half of which came from just 10 AI-linked companies, according to Bloomberg.

In a recent development, about 62% of Americans own stocks, either directly or through investments such as retirement accounts, according to a 2025 Gallup poll. Yet the wealthiest 10% of households hold 88% of the country's household stocks and mutual fund assets.

Industry observers note that in the San Francisco Bay Area's AI hubs, some of that AI-powered stock wealth has translated into an estimated $61,180 in additional down payment on a typical home, according to research from Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu. At the entry-level luxury tier, that premium reached nearly $200,000 in 2025.

The extra cash these buyers have brought to the market has allowed them to bid higher without taking on more debt, potentially displacing competitors into less expensive price brackets and driving up competition further down the market, Xu's earlier research suggests.

And so, what’s a barrier to entry for prospective buyers becomes a source of equity gains for existing homeowners—even those who have never invested in AI.

Annual home price growth now exceeds the national rate in all three markets where Xu identified signs of AI wealth bolstering down payments: Chicago (6.9%), Latest York City (5.8%), and San Francisco (3.7%), compared with 2.1% nationally, according to Tuesday's Case-Shiller release.

It’s an especially key point to make here because real estate wealth is more widely distributed than stock. Households between the 50th and 90th wealth percentiles hold nearly half of the country's household real estate assets, but just 11.4% of its stocks and mutual fund shares, according to second-quarter Federal Reserve data.

Homeowners in markets buoyed by AI wealth have, in effect, acquired a stake in the industry's stock market performance—whether or not they own any shares.

And the potential losses are enormous. To gauge their scale, Krugman looks to the so-called Buffett indicator, which measures the total value of U.S. stocks relative to the country's gross domestic product.

Before the recent sell-off, the ratio had climbed well above its peak during the dot-com bubble. AI-related companies accounted for nearly half of the S&P 500's market value and drove most of the increase in the indicator over the past several years, Krugman explains.

“If the Buffett indicator falls back to what it was in, say, 2019, that would wipe out wealth equal to around 80 percent of GDP: $25 trillion,” he wrote.

According to recent reports, and if his warning seems alarmist, consider what he wrote about the U.S. housing market in August 2005: “This is the way the bubble ends: not with a pop, but with a hiss.”.

More than two years before the onset of the Great Recession, Krugman identified falling sales and rising inventory as the early signs of a housing bust, as sellers struggled to command prices that buyers were no longer willing to pay.

Some of those symptoms are present today. In October, contract signings fell 17% annually while inventory grew 7.4%. Asking prices recorded their 12th consecutive month of annual declines, according to Realtor.com research.

Sources indicate that but the slowdown predates November's sell-off. Elevated mortgage rates and years of home price growth that outpaced wages have driven buyers to the sidelines, while many homeowners can afford to wait for better offers.

“On the seller side, we see more of a pause than an exodus,” Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, remarked earlier this month.

The question is whether an AI bust would produce another localized housing correction or a national downturn.

According to recent reports, “Generally speaking, the stock market and housing market can be connected, but usually not directly,” Krimmel explained amid an earlier bout of AI stock volatility in November 2025. “If they're moving together, that's typically because of some other outside force (could be driven by policy, Fed moves, and credit conditions, or a large macro shock) and/or because of changes in the job market.”.

To his point, when the dot-com bubble burst, the Nasdaq plunged more than 75% from its peak, wiping out trillions in paper wealth. Yet national home values continued to climb through the 2001 recession.

In San Francisco, however, home values fell 6.1% between February 2001 and January 2002, even as they rose 6% nationally, according to an analysis of seasonally adjusted Case-Shiller home price data.

The bigger question hanging over the housing market, though, is what an AI bust would mean for household spending.

According to recent reports, when households lose stock market wealth, they tend to spend less, even if their paychecks haven't changed—a phenomenon economists call the wealth effect. And just as stock market gains have held up demand for homes, they've also helped sustain demand elsewhere in the economy.

According to recent reports, any resulting pullback in spending, therefore, could end up rippling into layoffs in industries far removed from AI. Likewise, a slowdown in AI infrastructure investment could compound those losses, jeopardizing construction and manufacturing jobs in communities distant from Silicon Valley.

“Labor market softness is key for aggregate (and housing) demand,” Krimmel said last year.

And while the destruction of stock market wealth might initially dampen housing demand in a handful of affluent markets, rising unemployment could weaken it nationwide.

According to recent reports, during the dot-com bust, the Federal Reserve cut interest rates aggressively, helping sustain housing demand despite the economic downturn. Persistent inflation could complicate a similar response today.

“Lower interest rates will, in theory, help struggling companies' finances and allow them to keep existing workers, hire more, and/or provide pay raises to top performers,” Krimmel explained last November.

Recent findings suggest that access to credit could also become a problem. Tech companies are relying more heavily on corporate debt and private credit to finance their expansion, according to the European Central Bank's November Financial Stability Review. Losses on those investments could prompt lenders to tighten credit, making financing harder to obtain for homebuyers and builders alike.

The combination of falling incomes and more restrictive lending could depress home values in markets where AI wealth never drove them up in the first place.

But unlike during the Great Recession, a decline in home values would leave far fewer homeowners owing more than their properties are worth, limiting the risk of widespread foreclosures and the additional downward pressure on prices that forced sales can create.

In a recent development, “The typical homeowner today—and the housing market overall—is still well-positioned to withstand a correction without it turning into a crisis,” Krimmel said last November. “Home equity hit an all-time high in 2025Q2; mortgage holders are largely locked into sub-4% rates, giving them lower payments that are increasingly being eaten away by inflation. Very few homeowners are at risk of going underwater, even if prices were to decline 10% to 15%.”.

A year later, homeowner equity cushions remain substantial and mortgage delinquencies are low by historical standards, according to the Fed's November Financial Stability Report.

In a recent development, “Obviously, [a stock market crash] is not something anyone wants to see play out, and undoubtedly, if a stock market correction spilled over into the housing market, many homeowners would feel the pain,” Krimmel stated. “The silver lining of that hypothetical is that the knock-on effects would not be as severe. Luckily, the history of the housing bust and Great Recession would not repeat itself.”.

But for tens of millions of families, home equity is the college fund, the retirement plan, the safety net, and the most crucial source of wealth they'll ever build. The financial protections that could keep them in their homes during a downturn wouldn't necessarily protect that wealth.

When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year. Average hourly pay rose 3.1 percent.

Industry observers note that the October jobs report demonstrated employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace. Over the past year, the monthly payment on a median-priced home has climbed about three times as fast as average pay.

Sources indicate that the gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov. 6. The rate has remained within a narrow band of 4.1% to 4.3% since March, according to the BLS. The bureau also revised August and September up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38, a 3.1 percent gain over the year.

At October’s national median existing-home price of $416,700, a buyer putting 20 percent down would pay about $2,243 a month in principal and interest at this week’s average 30-year fixed rate of 7.11 percent, according to an Inman calculation. The same loan at the year-earlier rate of 6.24 percent would cost about $2,050. The difference is about $192 a month, or about 9 percent, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent.

The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 0.6 percent in September, BLS reported Nov. 10. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as did shelter.

The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point hike, according to the Fed’s statement. “But inflation is too high,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh mentioned in his press conference opening statement. The Fed meets again in December.

According to recent reports, adjusted for inflation, average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October, according to the BLS Real Earnings report. BLS said a 12-month comparison for October is not available because BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent from September 2025 to September 2026, according to the agency’s September report.

The number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October, according to BLS. These workers wanted full-time jobs but had their hours cut or could not find full-time work.

According to recent reports, the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11 percent for the week ending Nov. 12, up from 6.24 percent a year earlier, according to Freddie Mac.

In a recent development, existing-home sales fell 5.5 percent from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October, down 8.8 percent from a year earlier and the lowest pace since August 2010, Inman reported. Annual sales fell in all four regions, and the Northeast was the only region with a monthly decline.

According to recent reports, the median price rose 0.4 percent to $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7 from 107.3 a year earlier, and inventory reached 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.4 months in October 2025.

Forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share NAHB has reported since 2020, and 65 percent used sales incentives, according to the National Association of Home Builders. NAHB’s builder confidence index fell three points to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012.

The October data overall reveals an economy adding jobs at more than three times its 12-month average pace, while rates and prices keep pressure on buyer budgets. Agents can work from monthly payment figures and available concessions as tools to help keep transactions moving while the Fed weighs its December decision.

Australia-based Myriota Pty. Ltd., a global satellite platform for the industrial internet of things, today unveiled it has raised $40 million in the first portion of its Series C to launch next-generation satellites and accelerate customer adoption across international markets.

Recent findings suggest that main Sequence Ventures, Hostplus and Australia’s National Reconstruction Fund Corporation co-led the round. Funds SA joined as a latest investor. The round raised the firm’s total funding to more than $107.5 million, and is expected to close in early 2027.

Founded in 2015, Myriota’s platform makes satellite connectivity commercially viable for large-scale industrial IoT, using the same core technology to track mining equipment and trailers to also monitor fuel tanks, livestock water supplies and off-grid solar.

The manufacturer’s platform combines satellite connectivity, low-power devices, field installation tools and fleet management software to support existing infrastructure. The objective is to provide access to communication tools that connect what is in place with turnkey service, so a company can connect devices, machines and smart sensors no matter how remote they are.

“We’re at the beginning of a fundamental shift in industrial IoT,” Chief Executive Ben Cade remarked. “Industries increasingly rely on data from the field to make decisions about their operations, assets and resources, and as AI moves into the physical world, that data becomes even more essential.”.

The company expanded its platform over the past 12 months with the launch of HyperPulse, a global 5G non-terrestrial network, or NTN, and terrestrial service, and AssetHawk, a rugged, long-life asset tracker designed to make it economical to track industrial objects.

Industry observers note that alongside the expansion, it also grew into newly introduced verticals such as industrial fuels. It monitors and tracks fuel deployments across North America and Latin America, with EMEA and Asia Pacific to follow.

Industry observers note that myriota competes in a sector led by established operators such as Iridium Communications Inc., Orbcomm Inc. and Viasat Inc., alongside a growing field of providers pursuing cheaper, standards-based connections for industrial sensors and trackers.

The firm mentioned it intends to use the funds to expand its space infrastructure, including developing and launching its next-generation satellites.

Amazon Explicitly Bans Tiny Homes—Here’s How Sellers Are Sneaking $20K Prefabs Onto the Site Anyway

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As home prices and mortgage rates have climbed in recent years, homebuyers and developers alike have turned to factory-built tiny homes as a potential solution for affordable housing.
  • While low prices and fast shipping make prefab homes from Amazon look like a bargain, buyers should be aware of several factors with this purchase—starting with the fact that selling them is actually prohibited on the platform.
  • Amazon prohibits the sale of habitable tiny homes and prefabricated dwellings, with its Seller Central policy explicitly banning complete prefab homes, tiny house kits marketed as living spaces, modular and container homes, and other factory-built housing units.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As home prices and mortgage rates have climbed in recent years, homebuyers and developers alike have turned to factory-built tiny homes as a potential solution for affordable housing.

While low prices and fast shipping make prefab homes from Amazon look like a bargain, buyers should be aware of several factors with this purchase—starting with the fact that selling them is actually prohibited on the platform.

Amazon prohibits the sale of habitable tiny homes and prefabricated dwellings, with its Seller Central policy explicitly banning complete prefab homes, tiny house kits marketed as living spaces, modular and container homes, and other factory-built housing units.

So, why then does a search for "prefab tiny homes" bring up thousands of results?

That's because many are simple backyard sheds, compliant with the retailer's rules. Others walk a fine line.

Several listings, which fall between $20,000 and $25,000, use words like “prefabricated steel building” and “expandable modular container.”.

The highlights for one now unlisted item described it as “a portable, multi-purpose outdoor structure for storage, workspace, display, or commercial utility use.” It goes on to say that it has “versatile non-residential use—suitable for office setup, equipment storage, pop-up workspace, site unit, studio, or backyard utility structure.”.

Nowhere in the description did it call itself a home or use words like "residential" or "habitation.".

However, a flip through the photos revealed images of a warm and inviting interior—including a seemingly spacious bedroom. Potential layouts showed both one- and two-bedroom floor looks.

Realtor.com® reached out to Amazon for a comment on these listings but received no response.

Those looking to take the leap on a tiny home should still give local permitting requirements a close look. There is no single national zoning law for tiny homes in the United States, so buyers should check their local ordinances before purchasing.

Sources indicate that for example, in Los Angeles, tiny homes on permanent foundations, rather than wheels, are generally allowed, but each habitable room must be at least 150 square feet under the California Residential Code. Units must also meet all building code requirements for habitable space, such as proper ventilation and fire safety.

As long as owners receive the proper install and permits, owners can generally take out insurance on tiny homes, whether they serve as a primary residence or accessory dwelling unit like a detached studio or office.

In a recent development, “Insurance companies generally don't have issues with prefab homes, manufactured homes, or sheds. Most also don't have issues with an accessory dwelling unit on the site of a house,” Tom Firestine, founder of Longmeadow Insurance, tells Realtor.com. “When the local municipality allows them, we don’t have an issue extending coverage.”.

Recent findings suggest that regional weather differences raise distinct structural challenges for tiny homes. In Phoenix, extreme heat requires all units to have proper insulation and HVAC. While coastal regions contend with high winds, Firestine, who works out of Chicago, says their main concern is heavy snow loads.

“The biggest matter is whether the structure's install is permitted and how the use is presented to the insurance company,” says Firestine. “Intentionally misrepresenting something on an insurance application is the easiest way to get a claim denied. Insurers generally won't insure an illegal structure.”.

5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Real estate investing apps show the average return first.
  • Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building.
  • But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

Access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely shows you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

This fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

One had stopped going to the program’s update calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the manufacturer can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

Industry observers note that how to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same tech giant that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

Real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

Sources indicate that in real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

Industry observers note that if the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

Sources indicate that how to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

It has been revealed that say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

Sources indicate that now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

It has been revealed that how to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

It has been revealed that many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The company running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

How to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the company itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

Many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”.

It has been revealed that the lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”.

According to recent reports, how to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”.

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:.

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”.

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

Commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your proposal, not the floor under it.

The average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

In a recent development, amanda Neely is a Certified Financial Planner and the CEO of Counterflow. Connect with her on LinkedIn and Substack.

Breaking: Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1213 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.
  • Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules.
  • It has been revealed that the company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

It has been revealed that the company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it states can reach $15,000.

Sources indicate that the announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Industry observers note that sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson said in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”.

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Industry observers note that compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it mentioned already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the manufacturer.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson remarked.

MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter said.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

The newly introduced complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

On Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

On Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

It has been revealed that compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the glitch in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

In a recent development, on Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services.

He said Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the organization’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

The dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

Recent findings suggest that amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS announced plans for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

Sources indicate that in an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton said the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

The growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

Recent findings suggest that compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The company did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

Below is one of the 15 federal antitrust complaints filed by Compass against MLS organizations on Thursday. The lawsuits make similar legal arguments challenging restrictions on publicly marketing listings outside the MLS.

Tech Report: U.S. Home Prices Ticked Up 0.14% in October

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (612 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Redfin

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • home prices ticked up 0.14% month over month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis.
  • Sources indicate that prices rose 3.5% from a year earlier in October, the smallest increase since May 2026.
  • This is according to the Redfin Home Price Index (RHPI), which uses the repeat-sales pricing method to calculate seasonally adjusted changes in single-family home prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that U.S. home prices ticked up 0.14% month over month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis. That is the smallest increase in six months.

Sources indicate that prices rose 3.5% from a year earlier in October, the smallest increase since May 2026. Annual price growth has slowed for three straight months.

This is according to the Redfin Home Price Index (RHPI), which uses the repeat-sales pricing method to calculate seasonally adjusted changes in single-family home prices. The RHPI measures how sale prices of homes have changed since their previous sale—similar to the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Indices—but is reported about a month earlier. October data covers the three months ending October 31, 2026. Read the full RHPI methodology here.

Home prices continued to rise in October, but at a slower pace. Buyers gained more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records, which date back to 2013. Only three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas tracked by us were seller’s markets in October.

It has been revealed that however, a buyer’s market doesn’t necessarily signal strong buyer’s demand. “Mortgage rates are not that volatile right now, but they’re still higher than they used to be. That’s holding back demand and putting some downward pressure on prices, which have started to fall in many parts of the country,” noted Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics research. “On a national level, we don’t think prices will fall very much.”.

There’s also more supply available now, but sellers are not willing to cut prices deeply. “Many sellers are still anchored to the prices they’ve seen over the past few years, and because few sellers are under pressure to sell, that puts a floor under prices,” remarked Zhao.

Redfin tracks different types of home price trends. While our weekly and monthly housing market reports use the median home-sale price, which has recently shown a decline, the RHPI looks at repeat-sales prices of the same properties over time. It provides that isolates true underlying price appreciation rather than shifts in the types of homes selling, but because this is three-month moving average, it is also a slightly more “backward-looking view” according to Zhao.

Industry observers note that home prices rose in 30 of the 50 major U.S. metros month over month in October.

Industry observers note that the biggest increase was in Miami, where home prices rose 1.5% month over month on a seasonally adjusted basis. It’s followed by Montgomery County, PA (1.2%), Chicago (1.1%), Pittsburgh (1.0%) and Cincinnati (0.9%).

On a year-over-year basis, prices rose most in San Francisco, up 12.7%. It’s followed by Miami (11.3%), Chicago (9.5%), West Palm Beach (8.9%) and Philadelphia (8.5%).

The biggest price decline was in Seattle (-1.2% month over month). Next come Riverside (-0.7%), Detroit (-0.6%), Las Vegas (-0.6%) and Washington, DC (-0.5%).

Prices declined year over year in six major metros, four in Texas plus Seattle and Phoenix. San Antonio had the biggest drop (-3.0%), followed by Seattle (-2.1%), Dallas (-1.3%) and Austin (-1.1%). Houston (-0.2%) and Phoenix (-0.2%) also declined.

In a recent development, this report is part of Redfin’s monthly Home Price Index series. See all past reports and explore the latest data in the Redfin Data Center.

It has been revealed that our Mainland China operations are organized into three reportable segments: mainland China public securities, mainland China asset management, and mainland China insurance. Each segment operates under a dedicated brand and serves a distinct client need in the mainland China market.

Mainland China public securities.

Industry observers note that mainland China public securities, operating under the Noah Upright brand, is the business that distributes mutual funds and private secondary products in mainland China. This segment operates under an "online-first, offline-supported" business model, with the goal of facilitating global asset allocation through RMB-denominated products.

Mainland China asset management.

It has been revealed that mainland China asset management, operating under the Gopher Asset Management brand, is the business that manages RMB-denominated private equity funds and private secondary products. Current focus areas include managing primary market exits on existing vintages and growing cross-border ETF products in the secondary market.

Mainland China insurance, operating under the Glory brand, is the business that distributes insurance products in mainland China, consisting mainly of life and health insurance products. The business has been undergoing a strategic shift toward a commission-only broker model and comprehensive family succession planning services. The net revenues for the third quarter of 2026 were RMB1.3 million (US$0.2 million).

In a recent development, our international operations are organized into three reportable segments: international wealth management, international asset management, and international insurance and comprehensive services. The Tech giant operates booking centers in Hong Kong, Singapore and key U.S. markets including New York, Los Angeles and Silicon Valley.

International wealth management.

It has been revealed that international wealth management, operating under the ARK Wealth Management brand, is the business that provides offline and online wealth management services to global Chinese high-net-worth investors outside mainland China. At the moment we are dedicated to providing comprehensive services using our booking centers in Hong Kong and Singapore.

International asset management, operating under the Olive Asset Management brand, is the business that manages USD-denominated private equity funds and private secondary products, with a dedicated U.S. product center and partnerships with top-tier global managers across structured products and hedge funds. We are building our offices in Hong Kong, Singapore, Japan and key U.S. markets, including Upcoming York and Silicon Valley.

International insurance and comprehensive services.

Recent findings suggest that international insurance and comprehensive services, operating under the Glory Family Heritage brand, is the business that provides comprehensive international services such as insurance distribution, trust services and other family office-style services. With offices in Hong Kong, Singapore and Los Angeles, we provide global coverage to clients.

Headquarters reflects revenue generated from corporate operations at the Tech giant's headquarters in Singapore and office in Shanghai, as well as administrative costs and expenses that are not directly allocated to the aforementioned six business segments, including investments in platform-wide technology, AI infrastructure and corporate functions.

"In the third quarter of 2026, global markets became more volatile, and many high-net-worth clients shifted toward caution, liquidity and diversification," commented Ms. Jingbo Wang, Co-founder and Chairwoman of Noah. "We used this period to reposition the business. We stayed with our decision to step back from insurance distribution and put our resources into investment products and global asset allocation, where our long-term strengths lie. Even as markets pulled back, demand for our investment products held up, and our overseas business continued to deliver steady contributions.".

Industry observers note that "This quarter's results also include several one-off costs from streamlining our organization. We see these as investments in a leaner, more focused Noah.".

It has been revealed that "Building on the foundation we set out in the first half of the year, our use of AI is enhancing both the quality of our client service and the efficiency of our organization. It allows our relationship managers to serve more clients with greater consistency and helps our four global booking centers work together more seamlessly. Looking ahead, we will keep strengthening our global platform, risk management and technology capabilities to create long-term value for our clients and shareholders.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nearly 30 years after 6-year-old JonBenét Ramsey was found dead in her family’s home in Boulder, CO, the tragic case is regaining attention with the release of a new Netflix limited series.

“The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey” tells the story of the cold case through a lens that seeks not to solve the mystery, but to tell the story of those who were involved—particularly as the 1996 murder occurred in a decade marked by high-profile crime.

Industry observers note that the 1990s "ended with Columbine and started with the Menendez brothers, the Susan Smith murder, the OJ trial,” showrunner Richard LaGravenese noted in a statement. “I was fascinated by the challenge of doing something that was a murder mystery without an ending, without being solved.”.

To portray the effects of the media coverage that surrounded the case, the limited series will focus on Patsy and John Ramsey (played by Melissa McCarthy and Clive Owen) as well as a group of local and federal investigators (brought to life by Garrett Hedlund, Will Patton, Shea Whigham, and Alison Pill).

“They all had different points of view for all different reasons,” LaGravenese stated. “It was an incredible story to tell from all these perspectives.”.

The Ramsey family’s former home was at the center of the case, and although a handful of interior and exterior shots in the series’ trailer strikingly resemble the recognizable Tudor, it has been reported that “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey” was filmed in Calgary, Alberta.

Industry observers note that and while a few of the memorable details of the home—such as the black-and-white checkerboard tile floor in the kitchen—also make an appearance in the trailer, much of the home has been updated in recent years. Listing photos from 2024 show that the kitchen was entirely renovated.

Industry observers note that the Ramseys purchased the home for $500,000 in 1991, and moved to Atlanta in 1997 following JonBenét’s death. They sold the home for $650,000 in 1998, with profits from the sale pledged to the JonBenét Ramsey Children’s Foundation.

The 7,240-square-foot abode changed hands again, for $1.05 million in 2004. Numerous attempts to sell the home since then have come to naught. In 2008, it was listed for $2.68 million; the price was later reduced to $2.29 million in 2009, $2.3 million in 2011, and $2 million in 2014.

Sources indicate that nine years would pass before the home was listed again, asking $6.95 million in March 2023. After a series of price adjustments, the property was taken off the market in February 2025.

Recent findings suggest that jonBenét was found dead in the wine cellar in the basement of the home in the early hours of Dec. 26, 1996. Hours before her body was discovered, the family uncovered a ransom note in the home, which asked $118,000 for the return of their daughter.

Police determined she had been murdered in the late hours of the night on Christmas, and a later autopsy ruled the cause of death as strangulation.

In the following months, police investigated a number of suspects, including Patsy, John, and their son, Burke Ramsey—who were not cleared until July 2008, two years after Patsy died of ovarian cancer.

In a recent development, hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although XRP is at risk of losing its top-four position in the global cryptocurrency market, the asset still ranks among the three largest crypto assets in Japan.

In a recent post shared by the renowned Ripple-backed XRP treasury firm Evernorth, the company highlighted XRP’s growing performance in the Japan crypto market.

Earlier today, Evernorth shared monthly data from the Japan Virtual and Crypto Assets Exchange Association (JVCEA) revealing that XRP recorded about ¥132.8 billion in spot trading volume in September 2026.

While this accounted for about 15% of Japan's total crypto spot trading volume during the month, XRP emerged as the third most-traded cryptocurrency in Japan after Bitcoin and Ethereum.

This indicates that XRP has outperformed other major altcoins that are right now trading in the Japan crypto market, hitting about $880 million in trading volume.

While further data highlighted Solana and Dogecoin ranking next to XRP on the list as the fourth- and fifth-largest cryptocurrencies in Japan, respectively, the data also showed a wide gap from XRP’s ¥132.8 billion spot volume.

This means that XRP is significantly ahead of Solana and Dogecoin in the Japan crypto trading market, as Solana recorded only about ¥19.47 billion in trading volume during the same month.

Dogecoin, on the other hand, saw less participation, as it recorded only ¥11.27 billion in spot volume during the same period.

With XRP sitting in the third spot, the asset has become one of the most actively traded cryptocurrencies in Japan despite its persistent price volatility.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.delivered a record fiscal fourth quarter this week, roughly doubling its fiscal 2027 growth outlook, but its stock gave back nearly all of the prior day’s rally.
  • Fourth-quarter revenue rose 50%, to $14.5 billion, orders grew 88%, and adjusted earnings of $1.43 per share topped the high end of guidance.
  • Recent findings suggest that I joined a briefing with Chief Executive Antonio Neri and a small group of independent analysts shortly before the results came out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:27 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.delivered a record fiscal fourth quarter this week, roughly doubling its fiscal 2027 growth outlook, but its stock gave back nearly all of the prior day’s rally. The selloff suggests Wall Street still prices HPE as a low-margin server vendor, even though the results describe a networking and artificial intelligence infrastructure company with demand exceeding its ability to ship.

Fourth-quarter revenue rose 50%, to $14.5 billion, orders grew 88%, and adjusted earnings of $1.43 per share topped the high end of guidance. HPE now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to grow 27% to 35%, with adjusted earnings of $5.05 to $5.35 per share, according to its earnings release.

Recent findings suggest that I joined a briefing with Chief Executive Antonio Neri and a small group of independent analysts shortly before the results came out. Here are my four takeaways for investors and information technology leaders:.

Neri explained that networking orders grew more than 4.5 times faster than networking revenue in the quarter, up from 3.5 times the quarter before, and HPE exited the year with $10.5 billion in AI backlog.

Industry observers note that HPE doubled its networking purchase commitments over the summer and raised them again in the fourth quarter, but those components carry lead times of 28 to 40-plus weeks, so Neri expects networking conversion to pick up starting in the second quarter. Supply constraints are a better problem to have than weak demand, but they mean fiscal 2027 hinges on converting orders rather than winning them.

Industry observers note that the Juniper Networks integration is complete, and the annual cost-synergy target has risen to $800 million, but the bigger story remains the profit mix. Chief Financial Officer Marie Myers said networking will account for more than 40% of HPE’s operating profit by the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, up from less than a quarter of revenue. AI is a major driver, with routing orders growing by triple digits as customers connect AI data centers to one another.

Security was the soft spot, which Neri called “just timing.” When I asked whether the security portfolio is where he wants it as the industry consolidates around massive platforms, he argued for a different path.

“Fortinet and we have a different strategy — the convergence of security and networking — and we are taking it all the way down to the silicon level,” he stated. The convergence of networking and security is underway but will take time to execute, as a considerable amount of technical debt must go through its depreciation cycle. In a greenfield situation, organizations can easily deploy a converged solution, but in a brownfield environment, it requires much more work. This is the right strategy, but it remains a “prove-it” business for HPE.

Sources indicate that many neoclouds rely on vendor financing and chip-backed debt, raising real concerns about who is left exposed if the buildout slows. HPE says it has stayed out, and Neri was quite emphatic about it on the briefing.

“I want to be clear: We have not financed any neocloud through HPFS, our financing arm,” he said. “We have zero exposure to any AI financing for neocloud.” HPE has likely left some revenue on the table, but it drew the line in the right place. It will sell to neoclouds, as its $1.2 billion Vultr order highlights, without acting as their bank. Enterprise and sovereign customers account for the majority of its cumulative AI orders, and if the neocloud financing chain breaks, HPE’s financing arm won’t be the one holding the paper.

Training built the first phase of AI infrastructure, and Neri believes inference will build the next and will dominate demand for AI infrastructure. “I believe by the end of the decade, 80% will be in AI inferencing,” he stated. “Much of that will land on-prem. Much of that will be distributed, for sure. That’s why the server business is structurally well-positioned.”.

Once agents are in production, token costs become a recurring bill, and companies will want inference running alongside their own data. Those servers require far more memory and pull in storage and services, which is better business than racking graphics processing units for a hyperscaler.

Evidence of this is the interest in Helios, the Advanced Microdevices Inc. rack that uses HPE’s Ethernet switching rather than Nvidia’s proprietary interconnect. I asked Neri whether Jensen Huang’s brief departure from Nvidia Corp. had opened that door. He mentioned interest was building before then, as customers look to diversify.

HPE shares jumped 17% on Monday ahead of the report as part of a broader AI rally, then fell about 13% in early trading on Tuesday, ending near where they started the week. I see three reasons for this.

In a recent development, the first is margins. Cloud & AI operating margin was 18.4% in the quarter, and HPE guided to about 14% for fiscal 2027. Reuters reported that JPMorgan analysts called margin mix the key debate for investors.

Sources indicate that the second is pricing. Myers said higher selling prices have been the biggest driver of server growth, and she expects gross margin to moderate in the second half as AI server volumes ramp and costs rise faster than pricing.

The third is timing. HPE expects about 54% of revenue in the second half, with the ramp tied to Helios shipments, the Oracle Corp. deal, customer data center readiness and component supply. Those are fair execution questions, but they miss the shift in where HPE’s profit comes from.

On the topic of margins, the 18.4% came off an unusual stretch of favorable pricing that should not have been modeled as permanent. Neri argued the guide is still “significantly higher than any historical margin we have had in this business,” and he’s right outside the past year. A year ago, the segment’s margin was 9.3%. Margin rate also isn’t margin dollars. At 30% to 40% revenue growth, my math shows Cloud & AI adding well over $1 billion in operating profit at the midpoint.

The bears are right that price-driven server growth doesn’t warrant a premium multiple, which is why the mix matters more. The market is fixated on the segment whose margins are normalizing and ignoring the one whose margins are expanding. Adjusted earnings per share are still guided to grow by 27% to 35%, in line with revenue growth. That’s far from the margin doom-and-gloom narrative on the stock.

Industry observers note that the back-half concern is real but manageable. Myers described the pipeline as multiples of the backlog, and Neri mentioned the guide assumes only historical win rates against it.

Then there’s quality. HPE is guiding to about 30% growth and at least $5.5 billion in free cash flow, has no neocloud financing exposure and has already brought leverage below its target. It trades at about eight times the midpoint of its adjusted earnings guidance. “I don’t see us at a multiple that is 8 to 9x; it makes no sense whatsoever,” Neri stated on the earnings call.

For old HPE, that’s true, as it’s a server vendor, but HPE is increasingly a network vendor each quarter. In fact, during our pre-call with Neri, he led with networking and spoke at length about the business before pivoting to the server business. Expect networking to continue to drive a larger share of profits.

Sources indicate that fiscal 2027 is an execution year. HPE must convert purchase commitments into shipments, ramp Helios and prove that networking margins can climb even as cloud and AI margins settle. I’ll be watching networking order conversion more closely than server margins. If HPE executes, today’s multiple will prove to be too low.

Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that turn closings into case studies.
  • I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.
  • We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

In a recent development, I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

According to recent reports, most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to initiative. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

For years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

It has been revealed that we recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

It has been revealed that we eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

According to recent reports, I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

Not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Sources indicate that before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

It has been revealed that this has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

Recent findings suggest that I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

It has been revealed that what I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

It has been revealed that once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:.

Industry observers note that “Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”.

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

If you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a newly introduced closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

Sources indicate that there’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.
